items.body: Vertical London does exactly what it says on the can, establishing its premise from the very first minutes through a recording of birds and planes over Loughborough Junction. It is a sound I immediately recognised after spending twenty years living beneath the same flight path in South London, but Kate Carr approaches this familiar collision without lamenting noise pollution or searching nostalgically for a disappearing city. Birds and aircraft occupy the same acoustic plane, each accepted as part of London’s everyday ecology. From there, Carr moves through Tube stations buried beneath the city, the Greenwich Foot Tunnel, shopping centres, parks and lifts inside the Shard, eventually looking back down at London stretching and twinkling below. Verticality becomes a way of listening to the city across its different levels. Although the record follows a journey across the capital, it never feels like a collection of sonic postcards. London identifies itself only in passing, through station announcements, tannoys mentioning the River Thames or fragments of public transport. People are everywhere, yet they seldom become protagonists. Conversations remain indistinct, with voices often arriving through loudspeakers instead of direct encounters. Titles such as “I don’t think you can hear but people largely discussed dogs all the way back to central London” quietly acknowledge the limitations of field recording itself: microphones never quite capture the same experience as the person carrying them. One of the album’s greatest pleasures lies in its humour. Carr’s wonderfully verbose titles continually reshape the act of listening. “Celebrating a squeaky transport barrier…”, “A very long queue for the London Eye which is quite shit…”, or “It was New Year’s Day after all, and yes someone really was playing this at the overground station” all display a dry self-deprecation that gently punctures any temptation towards field-recording solemnity. The joke is never directed at the sounds themselves, but at the expectations we bring to them. The album takes listening seriously without ever taking itself too seriously. A loose temporal framework also runs through the work. New Year’s Day appears only through fleeting details: someone wishing “Happy New Year” in Bloomsbury, an unexpected instrumental rendition of “Auld Lang Syne” at an Overground station. There are no celebrations or drunken crowds. The city simply carries on, making the choice of date feel quietly counterintuitive. Carr documents a public holiday through a London seemingly suspended between one year and the next. The only explicit intellectual companion appears during the visit to Kilburn. At one point Carr quietly records herself (assuming it is her voice) saying the neighbourhood’s name, almost as if she were leaving a spoken geotag for reference. It has the feel of an aide-mémoire accidentally left in the finished work, but it also introduces Doreen Massey into the album. From this point, ideas about place begin to inform the act of listening itself. Massey’s understanding of place as something continually produced through movement, memory and social relations quietly echoes throughout the record. Every location remains connected to the next. High-frequency tones drift between recordings, drones appear among the crows and dinosaurs of Crystal Palace, and even Hampstead is characterised by the whisper imposed by private security and the sense of controlled space. London emerges as a continuum, its locations connected through sound and movement. What I admire most about Vertical London is its trust in ordinary experience. Carr never appears to chase spectacular recordings. The only “climax” arrives midway through with a couple of “high drama” moments which are anything but. Both “Dramatic build-up to when I dipped into the shopping centre to find a man playing piano outside Aldi” and “Dramatic drummers on the street as I ran due to being late for my Shard viewing platform booking” animate the narrative with suitably understated theatricality. Carr allows the city to reveal itself through patient walking, public transport, chance encounters and small acts of attention. A squeaking ticket barrier, electromagnetic harmonics from the DLR and birds beneath aircraft all receive the same careful consideration. By the end of the journey, landmarks have receded into a living acoustic fabric, where every layer—from the tunnels beneath the streets to the flight paths overhead—contributes to the city’s constantly shifting identity. To walks us through the album, we have asked Kate Carr to answer a few questions for us by email. You are a dedicated walker. One of your recent sonic explorations has been Transect – Heathrow perimeter walk with bird horns. You have circled London and frequently go on walks when traveling whether that might be in Italy or China. For this album, which is not strictly speaking just a walk as public transport is an integral part of it, you’re constantly moving between birds and planes over Loughborough Junction, the deep Tube stations, the Greenwich Foot Tunnel beneath the Thames, lift shafts inside the Shard, and eventually looking out over the city from above. What made you decide verticality was going to become the organising idea this time round? Has living under the flight pathway in a city with an extensive underground system made you more conscious of what’s above and what’s below, so to speak? And did you have any expectations of the sounds, frequencies, resonances you were going to find? I think ever since I did my album Midsummer, London a few years back and went across the city from one side to another on that long summer solstice day, I was sort of mulling what other sorts of trajectories I could trace. I was thinking about this vertical one for a while as it is obviously on the face of it a very different journey to moving across the city, and I suppose I wondered just how different it would actually be, both the experience of undertaking it and also how different it might sound within the recordings themselves. Movement and journeys are really central to my work, I am always asking: what version of this route is my movement producing in a recording, this combination of the chance elements, how I am recording, what gear I am using, my own personhood and identity and what or who I encounter. For a long while now I am interested in recording as a trace of how all those things come together, and what aural fragments of these encounters and moments is recorded or indeed not recorded by the in the recording device. In terms of time spent at different verticalities, I have spent a lot of time obviously on the tube as most commuters have, but comparatively very little in London’s higher reaches. In doing the album I was interested in if elevation could be heard somehow or other, can something sound higher up? Or lower down? And I was also interested in the zigzag journey I was undertaking to bring me to these various elevations in the city. So it was a few different layers or questions to the project. I think yes you are probably very right that living under the the flight path has influenced my thinking about the vertical, I was actually planning at one point that the highest point in the album might be a recording from inside a plane, but once I decided to do it on New Year’s Day this was shelved as an idea. The final component to the album as I was thinking about it revolved around the darkness of winter in London, I liked the idea of getting higher and higher, and closer to the sun as a way of gesturing towards the difficulties of this long dark period, and then this idea of the new year, new me sort of thing, and how the experience of new year’s day itself sort of punctures this. In the jumble of all these things the project lurks. Human presence is felt, as it is to be expected since this is an urban work, but it is not always discernible, the only distinct speech one can hear come from “institutional” sources, loudspeakers, recorded voices, or formulaic propositions. Is this because of ethical concerns or purely for compositional purposes? There are some voices in it, just snippets of people passing me, one person wishing another happy new year, and the sorts of murmurs you hear when moving through locations. I did not deliberately leave out conversations in this work, but I do have ethical considerations in regard to this issue. My practice is centred on the traces of activities, encounters, moments which unfold in public space, both ones I can be heard in and ones I am not. I think there is something of value in recording in public space in this sort of fragmentary and incomplete way, but that said there are of course conversations and encounters which I would choose not to use and would not consider it ok for me to use. In this case it was a cold, dark and quiet day, I was moving fairly quickly through locations and what reached me were just these small fragments. The work is meant to convey the experience of commuting and I guess purposeful movement rather than the drift of psychogeography. Of course as we move through public space we do sometimes get drawn into listening to other people’s conversations, but here the work is more about an experience of being in my own head and thoughts, while also encountering these fragments of other people also going about their days. One thing that really struck me is just how funny Vertical London is. Not because anything overtly comic happens, but because your titles quietly reframe what we’re about to hear. “Celebrating a squeaky transport barrier”, “A very long queue for the London Eye which is quite shit…”, “Dramatic build-up to when I dipped into the shopping centre to find a man playing piano outside Aldi…”—they all have this wonderfully dry, self-deprecating humour that somehow makes you listen more carefully rather than less. Field recording and sound art can sometimes take themselves rather seriously, yet Vertical London never does. It seems to embrace chance, anticlimax and the absurdity of everyday urban life without diminishing the act of listening itself. Do the titles emerge naturally from the walks, or have they become your way of gently keeping both the practice of field recording—and yourself—in check? Ha, well I am glad you found it funny. I do find humour just a really important component of basically just life. Not in a distancing way, or even in a not taking things seriously way but more just than humour and delight are part of the fabric of existence. I basically very often am quite astonished by people and what they do and say, and how different we all are from the smallest to the biggest things, and taking a trip and how this unfolds is no different. I find what people do, how they are in public space, how we encounter each other and organise ourselves sometimes just really charming, of course other times quite sad or even surreal. I think undertaking this very random project on New Year’s Day just sort of adds to that feeling. Here I am racing to these different parts of London for no real reason except to see what they sound like and what is happening in them, encountering all sorts of people doing their own things, and in all of that there are just really absurd and bizarrely anticlimatic moments, as well moment of rushing and drama. I don’t really feel I need to keep myself in check, or that sound art is too serious or takes itself too seriously, I just think humour is part of my orientation towards the world and others. I title the works after finishing the piece, but they come easily to me really. They just emerge from my memories of the day, both the felt memories and the narrative ones. I really like and enjoy the relationship between words and the sound work itself. I have always enjoyed that aspect of making work. I am basically obsessed with words, so I love to feel the dynamic between the composition itself and the words which accompany it and what this relation generates in terms of an experience of the work. What made you decide to set this work within a 24-hour timeframe, choosing New Year’s day as its anchoring point especially when Vertical London doesn’t feel particularly jubilant or hangover? I was going to possibly do it on the winter solstice so it matched my summer solstice work, and that would have been good as well, but I missed this date as I was busy I think and so I decided on New Year’s Day as I felt this trajectory of moving upwards resonated in quite interesting ways with ideas of new year’s resolutions, new starts, renewal. I did like the dry humour or irony which emerged in undertaking the work where this movement upwards was revealed as a shift into increasingly sterile, managed and privatised spaces. Increasing altitude does not prove revelatory or even particularly uplifting in this work. In terms of the day long time frame, I tend to work with these strict limitations nowadays because I like how the paucity of time infuses the work. It makes it difficult to position the work as an attempt at some sort of ‘portrait’ of London in a definitive way. The strictness of the protocol for me lends the work these connotations of the fragmentary, the gesture, the moment, the random, the arbitrary. In my work I am always seeking to emphasise: here is my journey, full of moments, charm, annoyances, yes absurdities and surreal slices of existence but it is not London itself, just one version of London authored in time, movement and space. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.album: Otto Taimela :: Cheap Ingredients (Cudighi)
items.excerpt: Taimela isn’t trying to recreate the 90s IDM and drum and bass golden era so much as he’s drawing a line from it to the present, letting those influences inform his melodic instincts without being consumed by them. items.body: Taimela isn’t trying to recreate the 90s IDM and drum and bass golden era so much as he’s drawing a line from it to the present, letting those influences inform his melodic instincts without being consumed by them. There’s a lightness to how he carries all of that reference—it never feels like homework, never feels like pastiche. It just sounds like a producer who grew up on the right records and internalized them so completely that they became his own vocabulary. Very thought out melodically, nostalgic at times, and beautifully crafted Cheap Ingredients by Otto Taimela   Finland has a particular relationship with electronic music that rarely gets the credit it deserves. The same quiet introspection that runs through the country’s classical and folk traditions has found its way into a generation of producers who make IDM and ambient work that feels rooted in landscape and weather rather than dancefloors or scenes. Otto Taimela is one of the most versatile of them—a pianist, composer, sound designer, and producer based in Finland with a discography that refuses categorization, moving between avant-garde piano, breakbeat, ambient techno, and neo-classical composition across labels like SWIMS, Cold Blow, Ultraääni, Special Species Records, and Cudighi Records, the LA-based label run by Ben Van Howe that focuses on international psych, art pop, ambient, and electronic music. This is Taimela‘s second release on Cudighi following 2024’s A Life, and it’s the most coherent statement of his IDM-facing side yet. Cheap Ingredients is a good IDM release and a genuinely cute one—cute in the sense that the sounds and melodies composed through this album are lovely, catchy, and beautiful to listen to. The album plays consistently well as a flow of old-school breakbeats and drum styles with beautiful pads and keys throughout. As uncanny as the cover looks, what appears to be two Mickey Mouse-like characters standing next to a palm tree, drawn in a deliberately naive hand, it doesn’t match the aesthetic of the music at all, which makes it strangely interesting. The music overall sounds very thought out melodically, nostalgic at times, and beautifully crafted. The genre here sits closer to drum and bass IDM than anything else—not drill and bass, which is more aggressive and abstract in structure, and not liquid drum and bass, which is softer and more melodic in the conventional sense. This has an abstract structure to it while maintaining real warmth in the low end subs. “VCXO” is a prime example of good bass sub usage and chill, not too fast, not too slow, just good downtempo electronica. The melodies and atmospheres here hit somewhere between Roni Size‘s early drum and bass work and the melodic sensibility of Plaid, two reference points that don’t often share the same sentence but make complete sense here. Standouts: “Glacier,” “New Life,” “Spell 3,” and “Formal Mass.” “Spell 3” is particularly hypnotizing in its ambience and loop, it recalls the old school Boards of Canada loops that take you off guard, the kind that don’t announce themselves as special until you realize you’ve been inside them for longer than you expected. “Bullfinch Nest” exposes beautiful vocal warble work coming in every four to eight bars, it sounds like a bird, or the reminiscence of one, and when the pads arrive alongside it the combination becomes catchy in a way that’s hard to shake. Whatever that sample is, it’s the character of the track. It recalls Aphex Twin‘s “Slow Bird Whistle” from the Peel Sessions in concept — not in sound, not in execution, but in the specific idea of a non-musical element becoming the personality of a piece. Very well done. “Mysterious Thing” is a wonderful interlude, the vocal sample and record-rewinding effect being tossed into the playing melody is fantastic to listen to. It’s not turntablism—it’s something closer to the small, playful interludes that appeared on early Plaid releases, or the kind of moment that Mr. Oizo delivered on Analog Worms Attack (1999)—those brief, almost comedic left turns that humanize an otherwise electronic record. This would be the drum and bass version of that instinct, and it works perfectly. The album grows on you with each listen. It really is hard to choose between tracks because the more time you spend with it the more it reveals. A golden egg of classic sounds and nostalgia, one of those releases that knows exactly what era it’s drawing from and has the skill to make it feel fresh rather than imitative. Taimela isn’t trying to recreate the 90s IDM and drum and bass golden era so much as he’s drawing a line from it to the present, letting those influences inform his melodic instincts without being consumed by them. There’s a lightness to how he carries all of that reference—it never feels like homework, never feels like pastiche. It just sounds like a producer who grew up on the right records and internalized them so completely that they became his own vocabulary. Cheap Ingredients is exactly what the title doesn’t suggest—carefully considered, melodically rich, and worth every return listen. Cheap Ingredients is available on Cudighi. [Bandcamp] The post Otto Taimela :: Cheap Ingredients (Cudighi) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Machine listening is transforming environmental sound into data points that support surveillance infrastructure, changing what it means to hear, argues Stephen Roddy in The Wire 512 On 28 February 2026, Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school in Minab, Iran was hit by a missile killing over 150 people, most of them children. Initial investigations have suggested that the US was responsible for the attack. While US data mining giant Palantir has not been conclusively linked to the atrocity, the wider US-led bombing campaign has made extensive use of the Palantir-supplied Maven Smart System to coordinate similar attacks. Maven can combine large volumes of data from radar, satellite, communications and even audio sources before applying machine learning techniques to identify possible military targets. We now live in a world where our homes, schools and workplaces can become clusters of data points. According to James Parker, academic and Earshot board member (see The Wire 499), machine listening integrates audio and machine learning systems to monitor, analyse, govern and modulate human and nonhuman systems through computational renderings of the soundscape. As these systems proliferate globally, they represent an imperial mode of decision making and environmental governance that is in conflict with the basic tenets of democratic accountability. Who owns and governs these systems? Who or what do they hear, and what remains unheard? Who acts upon the claims these systems make about the world? Machine listening effectively expands the reach of these systems into the realm of the audible, proliferating throughout contemporary soundscapes: classifying gunshots, indicators of distress or aggression in human voices, and sounds associated with intrusion across borders and within protected spaces. Far from being neutral descriptors of a soundscape, these classifications are political, and operational categories and their detection can trigger responses from security or police forces and mark individuals for further surveillance. Flock Safety, the surveillance tech company drawing ire for its operation of video and audio detection networks across the US, recently pulled plans to listen for indicators of “human distress” across their audio network due to strong opposition from civil liberties groups like the Electronic Frontier Foundation. Across Europe, comparable systems are already deployed in public spaces, transport lines and security networks in London, Groningen and Plzeň. In a political moment defined by the convergence of private technological infrastructure with authoritarian state power, ubiquitous machine listening networks increasingly provide companies, states and militaries with acoustic classifications upon which they can act. What becomes of listening in such times? Almost 50 years ago, composer and writer R Murray Schafer helped to establish the field of acoustic ecology around a central opposition between the lo-fi soundscapes of urban, industrial and mechanised life, in which dense noise acts to mask and corrupt clear and meaningful acoustic signals, and the hi-fi soundscapes he associated with the natural world. One unintended political consequence has been to allow the soundmaking activities of communities, often marginalised by race and class living and working in urban environments, to disappear into noise. This is not helped by the disturbing resonance between his oft-cited claim that “the world suffers from an overpopulation of sounds” and the eugenicist overpopulation tropes circulating throughout Western environmentalist thought of the 1970s. The troubling concept of nature, as inherited from Schafer and his contemporaries, is usefully dismantled and reconstituted from a field recording perspective in Mark Peter Wright's Listening After Nature, in which he illustrates how nature is constituted by material interrelationships between culture, technology, place and practice. Wright’s guiding question, “What am I not hearing?”, surfaces the human lives, labour and infrastructural relations that are often concealed in the production of field recordings. The emerging ubiquity of machine listening further complicates this problem. Decisions are now made and actions taken on the basis of features extracted from audio signals. What cannot be heard, captured and classified is excluded from the systems account of the world and becomes operationally non-existent. Conversely, audio that does not fit the systems’ predefined categories for the world can become misclassified; and as the strike on Minab illustrates, misclassification within these systems can have devastating effects. Is this pattern of low rumbling a harmless passing vehicle or an intrusion? Is that high energy transient a firework or a gunshot? What about this repeating pattern of falling frequencies – is that a barking dog or a human in distress? Classifications like these are bundled with other data like time, location and contextual information before triggering an alert, providing a recommendation or, in some cases, initiating an automated response. The sounds involved need never be listened to by human ears before being converted into operational data to support systems of classification and control. These questions are explored by Machine Listening, a platform for collaborative research and artistic experimentation, in Environments 12. The project is a speculative extension of a popular series of 11 environmental records released by Irv Teibel between 1969–79. It explores a future Earth in which a developing cybernetic ecology powered by planetary-scale computation has laced microphones and loudspeakers throughout the biosphere, automating the reproduction, synthesis and management of the soundscape. Dynamics of capture, identification, classification and data-driven intervention are stretched almost to breaking point across the 15 short but richly textured sonic works. Human voices vault and bounce in cacophonous chorus alongside their generative clones amid lush field recordings. Organic life and human technology are almost indistinguishable from one another as a planetary machine listening infrastructure feeds the soundscape back to itself in a continuous cycle of replication. Where Schafer feared technology might mask nature, and Wright showed how it can constitute it, Environments 12 imagines nature to be continuous with data and deeply entangled with the infrastructures that detect and manage it. But the world imagined by the project is already being built. Listening after Palantir cannot be about a return to some imagined innocence or a retreat into Schafer’s idealised nature. Critical listening must instead focus on machine listening itself – exposing the classifications it imposes, the infrastructures in which it is embedded, and the power relations that shape its production and deployment. It must not only ask what the machine cannot hear, but what it has misheard, and who will suffer as a result. This essay appears in The Wire 512. Wire subscribers can also read it in our online magazine library.

items.album: Tom Templar on Digging Graveyards
items.tags: experimental electronic jazz world psych prog
items.excerpt: Peter Ross talks to the Green Lung frontman about the 'Magnificent Seven' graveyards of London, and transcending fear of death. Main photograph taken in Barnes Old Cemetery At Green Lung gigs, frontman Tom Templar has a particular way of introducing the band: “We play Old English, black magic, forest-dwelling, mushroom-eating, goat-bothering, devil-worshipping heavy fucking metal.” It is a neat summary of their aesthetic, though he might add “graveyard-visiting” as that is part of the vibe, too.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — It truly feels otherworldly, a blend of metal guitar, progressive rock, and chamber music, alongside something that defies words and enters (fortunately) an ethereal musical realm. The lineup chosen by Ian Alexander, a guitarist born in Cologne, Germany, features two drummers, a vibraphonist, and a harpist. This lends a unique, personal atmosphere to the album; while Alexander has always sought to express his deepest passions in his solo work, here they manifest in a distinctive way. On tracks like "Tau Librae," the guitar sounds heavily distorted at times, yet by the time we reach "Electric Water Experience," the arpeggios take flight, evoking pure fusi�n, albeit of an experimental nature that feels both familiar and strange. It is like those sci-fi movies where someone we know is replaced by a body double that looks exactly the same... yet something feels "off." In this case, however, there is no jarring noise, only excellent, highly dynamic, and hypnotic music. Alexander found the perfect vehicle and the right "bodywork" to convey the emotions he intended, even when they might seem contradictory; ultimately, because they spring from the same soul, they do not conflict, but rather make as much sense as melody and harmony themselves.Clairvoyance resonates with echoes and hints of space rock; the harp and drums form an ideal pairing, balanced by a guitar that, at will, introduces calm, stillness, and repose. Alexander explores various styles throughout the album; the sound can evoke vast open plains one moment, yet feel claustrophobic the next, like climbing an endless spiral staircase in an early 20th-century novel. At times, the music turns powerful and almost funk-like, then scales upward, building tension through the magic of electric guitar textures, later joined by the vibraphone. Each track is unique; on "Attack of the Android Jester," Alexander plays bass, delivering an infectious groove that suddenly shifts into strange frequencies mimicking electronic sounds, all while a beautiful progressive passage gradually takes shape. Jazz-rock fusion resurfaces, as it does whenever Tau Librae performs, with compositions so accomplished they speak to Alexander's maturity as both a songwriter and a performer."Mothership" begins with an almost electronic feel, underpinned by a jazzy drum foundation reminiscent of Weather Report; the dual-drummer setup is noticeable, and a certain dissonance contributes to an eerie atmosphere that never actually undermines the melody.The classic harp format is utilized at the start of "Windowpane / Courage and Corrosion", evoking a different sense of time, a moment of carving out a space and dwelling there. Those produced echoes linger longer, like a stone skillfully skipped across a lake. Eastern tradition meets Western as the track enters its second section, a modern epic, if such a term applies, representing the new language Alexander sought, and suddenly the album's title, "The Nineteenth Star of the Libra Constellation," takes on a new meaning, reflecting that drive to pull us from our comfort zone and transport us to somewhere entirely new.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Much has been written about this album, and much more will be, since ultimately, it is up to each listener to decide which era they enjoy most; that is precisely what makes it valuable. However, if we are to exchange impressions, I must say that as a lifelong Jethro Tull fan, I really liked Too Old to Rock 'n' Roll: Too Young to Die! just as it is. Simpler in structure and composition than its predecessors, it completes an arc spanning the entire decade of the 70s, moving from raw blues and jazz to elaborate progressive rock, and then (following Minstrel in the Gallery as the swan song of their grand epics) continuing with a run of solid albums featuring acoustic folk-rock and flute-driven rock, leading up to Stormwatch in 1979.The recording style itself featured a distinct, more modern vocal echo; the string arrangements on "Quizz Kid" were just as classic as those they had used previously, and Ian Anderson's voice remained in perfect form'though now serving songs of a simpler construction that drew partly from 50s rock while also incorporating classical influences. The brass section added a fresh tone, and whenever a song shifted to a slower section, the arrangements remained delicate and intricate, evoking old waltzes that coexisted with a modern sound hovering somewhere between glam and new wave. Yet, somehow, they made it all work for me, Martin Barre's guitar, Ian's flute, and a band sounding incredibly tight.I have a real soft spot for "Crazed Institution," and I always loved how they blended the bass and acoustic guitar. They were really playing around with the arrangement, electric guitar appearing and fading out, piano coming in and dropping away. "Salamander" captures the full power of Barre's guitar, a perfect counterpart to Ian's vocals, and traverses so many musical landscapes and tonal colors before the singing even begins; it is a marvel to listen to. How, then, can anyone say the album doesn't measure up? When they started out, they dressed like rag-and-bone men, wandering alleys with dogs, wearing little more than an old overcoat or a bowler hat; later came the capes and tights, so why couldn't they change again? To me, it was a very dignified shift where the quality of the music remained intact; it was their signature style, without ever betraying who they were."Taxi Grab" has a vibe that sits somewhere between Western and glam; it sounds like classic Tull, bluesy, yet also modern and cool. Not to mention the variety of styles Barre executes, along with the subtle variations where they played with and subverted the genres they were channeling. These moments are scattered throughout, waiting to be discovered by anyone willing to look for them."From A Dead Beat To An Old Greaser" has the same ingredients as songs from the past but is modernized with a Rhodes keyboard and a saxophone that comes in later; there's a touch of country-western, too, yet it ends up sounding jazzy, almost like cabaret music. To me, they pull it off very naturally, partly because of the strings, which pair perfectly with Ian's vocals. John Glascock's bass playing proves fundamental to the album's sound."Bad-Eyed and Loveless" has a flamenco touch; Barre's acoustic guitar and Anderson's vocals shine, enhanced by that echo effect that suited them so well, creating space through silence in introductions that could stretch on indefinitely, as they never repeated in the same way throughout the song. Beyond technical quality, they held something else for me: genuine feeling, the other essential ingredient of music. "Big Dipper" featured subtle details tucked into the chorus alongside John Evan's piano, paving the way for "Too Old to Rock 'n' Roll: Too Young to Die", the album's title track, a signature song, and a virtual statement of principles that instantly became a new classic for the band. I remember the Tampa, Florida show, not because I was there (I was just being born around that time!), but because I've seen the footage and witnessed the deep emotion with which these songs were performed. Like the tracks on the albums that followed, they resonated powerfully with me, marking a distinct, intense phase in the band's evolution. The 50s rock 'n' roll format intersects with classical elements, where wind instruments and guitar engage in Bach-like counterpoint, and strings come together to create an unforgettable song that is 100% Tull."Pied Piper" is another great acoustic gem, overflowing with ideas and subtle melodies from a flautist who keeps one foot in the forest and the other on the city pavement. A classic chorus would emerge out of nowhere, with his magnificent voice gracing every song; at times his singing would quicken, making it a delight to hear alongside the pizzicato violins.Perhaps "The Chequered Flag (Dead or Alive)" could be considered a concession to a more commercial sound... yet it also features classical echoes and a magnificently integrated string section, all full of emotion. So, for me, Too Old To Rock 'n' Roll: Too Young To Die! will always be an album that warms the heart, in a different way from its predecessors, certainly, but also marking the start of a new and equally great era of albums that would last until the end of the decade.

items.body: Review by ianjferris@gmail.com — Last week, at a small record & cd fair in a little community based local hall in County Wicklow, I flicked through a sale bin of old records. Three albums therein caught my attention - Olias Of Sunhillow by Jon Anderson, Hergest Ridge by Mike Oldfield and Five Bridges by The Nice (the subject of this review). All were in excellent condition and I secured the three for ?20. Olias of Sunhillow (particularly) and Hergest Ridge were excellent purchases. Five Bridges however, is just not my cup of tea. I completely understand Keith Emerson's talented approach to this album but really, it's contents are just overbloated self indulgent piffle, much in the same vein as the later Pictures at an Exhibition, which was also helmed by Emerson In Chief. While Five Bridges isn't without a few brief nice moments (pun completely intended), the fact is they are just that, a few brief moments. So it's not for me. Sorry to all you Nice fans out there but it's just 2 stars (it would have been one star except for the fact that when I awarded only one star to Pictures At An Exhibition, Progarchives wouldn't publish my review 😊 - probably right too because it was a bit scathing). Collectors, dedicated fans and completionists only. I hope to offload the album soon, to a shop in Dublin which deals secondhand records.

items.body: Review by Hector Enrique — Led by its frontman and multi-instrumentalist, Christofer Johnsson, Therion dedicates "Secret of the Runes" (2001), its tenth album, to exploring the mysteries of Yggdrasil: the enormous sacred tree that occupies a central place in the Norse worldview and around which the nine worlds are arranged. The concept is rooted in the fascinating Norse mythology, as transmitted by medieval sources that preserve much older traditions. An album shrouded in the misty, mystical, and legendary aura inspired by gods, giants, humans, and elves, it is grounded in symphonic metal with a distinct neoclassical element and serves as a starting point for delving into the various branches of the metal genre found within the Swedes' broad and shadowy sonic spectrum.Thus, the intricate choral, orchestral, and operatic arrangements of the thirty or so guest musicians blend harmoniously with Kristian Niemann's powerful and sophisticated guitar riffs and solos, both in the death metal elements of the majestic "Ginnungagap" -which opens the way to the chaos of the primordial void of creation and is surely one of the album's best tracks- as well as in the depths of the doom-laden "Jotunheim," the black-metal darkness of the lugubrious "Nifelheim" and "Helheim," and the power-metal-style bursts of energy in the fast-paced "Asgard" and "Muspelheim."And that sense of persistent tension and chaos conveyed by the most extreme and dense tracks finds gradations in the more progressive "Schwarzalbenheim" and a breath of fresh air both in the serene "Midgard" - which refers to the realm of humans and is another of the album's major themes - and in the folk-metal interludes of the celestial "Ljusalfheim" and the pastoral "Vanaheim." All of this comes together to form an album with a wide range of nuances that mesh seamlessly, which the title track "Secret of the Runes" sums up as an operatic compendium and a very fitting concluding epilogue.An excellent album that, along with "Theli" (1996) and "Vovin" (1998), represents one of the highest peaks of compositional and musical maturity in the band's entire career, as well as establishing itself as a cornerstone of symphonic metal.4 stars

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — Some 36 years in and still going strong. The now legendary SIGH has become nearly synonymous withJapanese avant-garde metal with a knack for melding the most unlikely of sounds together in acohesive whole and still finding new ways to take the fanbase somewhere the band has not yetexplored. Once again the crazed black metal turned experimental sonic wizards led by the inimitableMirai Kawashima returns with its 14th release GOH-KA, another hi-brow conceptual masterwork thattranslates as something akin to "infernal fire scorching the sinners" or simply "karma." The albumdelves into the darker concepts of Buddhism including the concepts adapted from the Buddhist hellscrolls and through a series of 11 tracks this team of five presents a fiery hellish journey thatforges a fiery path through the crossroads of bands such as Celtic Frost, Voivod, second wave blackmetal and traditional Japanese music.It's the usual maelstrom of anything goes in the SIGH universe although GOH-KA retains the morefocused approach of tightly woven concept albums of recent years. You can expect the usualthunderous roar of black metal guitar works along with a pounding bass and drum accompaniment butSIGH delves deep into its Japanese heritage with ample traditional instruments woven into the mixalong with moments that eschew the metal paradigm completely with large chunks of "Anzenshokon" forexample sounding more like a movie soundtrack before trading off with the first wave black metalapproach that has been its bailiwick since its inception. Joining the SIGH team is bassist Fr�d�ricLeclercq (Kreator, Dragonforce), ex-Fear Factory drummer Mike Heller and Opeth mastermind Mikael�kerfeldt who delivers a ripping guitar solo on "Unputenpu" the album's lead single.SIGH traverses these brackish waters well and with the opening "Kuso-shi (1-3)" runs the gamut ofcrafty psychedelic rock laced avant-metal with epic classic Japanese traditionals interwoven into araspy narrative that together generate interesting melodic developments, stylish fusionfunctionality and epic transitions between varying stylistic approaches. Perhaps a mellower lessmetal dependent release from previous works but an effective expansion of the sonic palette whereatmospheric embellishments are allowed to shine like diamonds in the rough. The one constant that isthe thread between all SIGH albums are the raspy vocals of Kawashima's feisty spirited lyricaldelivers however there are many more backing vocal additions which give this album a much largerthan life production value. As always many metal purists may not deem GOH-KA as metal enough butlike many of SIGH's constructs, the metal is merely one vital ingredient to a much larger sonicedifice. Somewhat reminiscent of the band's best known release "Imaginary Soundscape," GOH-KA delivers asimilar kaleidoscopic approach where psychedelia, metal, traditional folk and progressive symphonicrock play together like Bambi and Godzilla in a universe of the band's own making and once againsomehow despite all the odds stacked against the whole shebang comes off as yet another triumphantvictory for this Tokyo based band that continues to punctuate the 21st century with some of the mostcutting edge sounds under the greater banner of metal music. Personally i find the expanded use oftraditional Japanese instruments and homegrown flavors to be the wise choice for this creative bandto delve into. Metal and folk music has been immensely popular for over three decades now but yetthe Japanese have been more reticent to traverse these developments however SIGH proves it has thechops to pull it all off with ease. Another excellent release from Tokyo's wildest metal band.

items.body: Review by martindavey87 — I can't really dwell on this one for too long, it pretty much is what it says it is. Most of these songs are demos and as such, the quality reflects that. Although, they're fun to hear the progress of the writing, especially with 'Inferno', where vocalist Russell Allen replaces unfinished lyrics with a random "do do dooooo" (just as you're getting into it and preparing to belt out the actual lyrics at the top of your voice!). And then of course, there's the 'Star Wars Suite' and a demo of the unreleased track 'Disillusioned'. 'Disillusioned' is a decent track which would have fit perfectly on the bands' first album, and the Star Wars song, well, is what it is. I love Symphony X, and if you're a die-hard fan like me, this is actually a very cool disc (especially since there's some dodgy unofficial versions floating around now, which admittedly does have much better artwork), and while it's nothing you'd ever really choose to listen to more than a couple of times, it's still a worthy addition to the collection.

items.body: Review by kenethlevine — While one can never accuse JOANNA NEWSOM of adopting conventional voice and arrangements on a path to surprisingly broad cult acceptance, "Divers", still her most recent, is refreshingly accessible in both arenas. While she has retained her core idiosyncrasies, since "Have one on Me" her retooled pipes, emphasis on more conventional song structures and reliance on a more expansive instrumental palette have allowed what was always there to emerge more plainly, from the Celtic harp inspirations to the Appalachian allusions, and, yes, a little bit country. The centerpiece title cut argues best for this successful evolution in a progressive context, beginning with her unabashed plucked intro and mysterious airs, while "Leaving the City" among others sports her evolution into rapid-fire meters, even if the end of the closer is an overly over the top example. Other standouts are the earthier "The Things I say" and "Same Old Man", the earworm "You will not take my heart alive", and especially "A Pin-Light Bent", which sounds like Joanna guesting on an early IAMTHEMORNING number, that is, sublime.While Joanna isn't ever for the musically unadventurous chart gazers, "Divers" is probably the best place to get your feet wet before plunging deeper with abandon, an activity I fully endorse.

items.body: Review by tupan — I am not much of a review guy, but after listening to the fourth VISCERA/// album several times, I think I need to give my two cents! VISCERA/// (yep, the three slashes are part of the name) is a italian band that began its career playing grindcore/goregrind in the early 00's, but soon moving to atmospheric sludge in their debut. This one is their fourth full lenght (don't counting two collaboration albums), and was released this year by Time to Kill Records. The music is a refreshing mix of atmo sludge, grunge, prog and many nods to post-punk from the eighties. The vocals change from harsh black metal shrieks to clean Jaz Coleman (from KILLING JOKE fame) inspired singing! I really recommend this album, one of the best surprises of 2026. Check it out!

items.body: Review by alainPP — Cambrian evokes Symphony X and Dream Theater, blending progressive metal and death metal with screamed vocals."What Lies Beneath - Pt. 1" opens with the sound of surf, Gregorian whispers, and a dark, vulnerable spoken-word passage. Crystal-clear piano, high-pitched vocals, and a solemn tone set the cinematic stage. "Rules of Engagement" explodes with heavy drums driving feverish keyboards; Epica-style growls meet Freek's snarling vocals, while the rhythm section allows for both intense passages and melancholic, My Dying Bride-esque moments featuring a solemn organ of despair. A highlight is the delicate piano outro accompanied by a distressed, screaming vocal. "Locked Room Murder Mysteries" begins with arpeggios before unleashing screamed vocals over neo-prog keyboards?a successful blend. This multi-layered fusion of heavy aggression and swirling keyboard work makes one forget the story's cruelty. There's a sudden hint of Anathema; the vibe is a plus, though the nasal vocals are a downside, wavering between melody, doom, and restrained violence."Requiem for Innocence" serves as an atmospheric intermezzo driven by emotional piano; the swelling melodic crescendo paves the way for the dramatic "Oceans Away," featuring razor-sharp riffs, machine-gun percussion, and fiery keyboards layered with a Balkan accordion. Lennart's class shines through in this track?at once festive and cruel?a melancholic folk ode set against a djent backdrop, featuring a solo reminiscent of Jordan Rudess and a spine-tingling keyboard-guitar duel."Shards of a Broken Mirror" channels Dream Theater with its musical opulence and richness. Freek drives the narrative forward as the instruments flood the senses with progressive metal that?with its extreme growls?bears the unmistakable scent of Opeth. The fusion might unsettle purist prog fans, yet the solemn keyboard-and-vocal breaks serve as a reminder that the prog spirit runs deep. A long, atmospheric acoustic outro gives way to the sudden arrival of "Last Man Standing"?cut from the same cloth, featuring grand, soaring keyboards set against metronomic drumming. The sound is both ominous and divine, an all-encompassing "liturgical metal" experience; the languid vocals?hovering between singing and narration?evoke Light Damage, while the sacred fire, double-kick drumming, and layered growls bring Epica to mind. A vehement track, dripping with narrative drama and neoclassical keyboards, reminding us that beneath every metalhead lies years of music theory training. "Requiem for Guilt" unfolds toward the finale, with spoken vocals drifting over airy keyboards before a powerful surge?a razor-sharp riff cutting through luminous synth lines. The atmospheric fusion, enhanced by a piano break, crystallizes the mood; tension builds like a lava-filled crater awaiting an imminent eruption. An Anathema-style finale follows, offering gentleness alongside a fleeting guitar solo. "What Lies Beneath - Pt. 2" brings the story to a close?sometimes, is it better not to reveal the truth? A melancholic, atmospheric finale turns the final page.Cambrian spent eight years crafting this album, a blend of neoclassical passages, growls, and progressive, atmospheric, and doom-laden breaks; it is classic, sprawling progressive metal?though its tendency to pack in too many ideas proves to be its Achilles' heel. (3.5)

items.body: Laibach released “WAT” on 8 September 2003 through Mute Records. The album turns 23 this year. Iztok Turk and Laibach produced the record, with Umek co-producing and sharing mixing duties with Turk; Nilesh Patel handled mastering at The Exchange. The track “Anti-Semitism” was separately produced and mixed by Temponauta. “WAT” is an acronym for “We Are Time,” revealed on the title track. Laibach has described the album’s intent as being not about “what Laibach is, or what it wants, but what you are and where you stand.” What is on Laibach’s ‘WAT’ The CD edition runs 12 tracks: “B Mashina”, “Tanz mit Laibach”, “Du bist unser”, “Achtung!”, “Ende”, “Now You Will Pay”, “Hell: Symmetry”, “Das Spiel ist aus”, “Satanic Versus”, “The Great Divide”, “WAT” and “Anti-Semitism”, with a total running time of 58:23. The 2LP vinyl edition replaces “Now You Will Pay” in its track sequence with the bonus cut “Reject or Breed” and runs 62:27. The CD also carries an enhanced video for “Tanz mit Laibach”. Tomi Meglič of Siddharta contributed music, lyrics and additional vocals on “B Mashina”. Long-time NSK collaborator Peter Mlakar wrote lyrics for “Du bist unser” and “Achtung!”. Slavko Avsenik Jr. arranged the choir parts and co-wrote the title track, and Matej Mršnik played guitar on “Ende”. “Tanz mit Laibach” was released as a single on 25 August 2003, with remixes by Umek, Johannes Heil, Zeta Reticula and Temponauta, and an accompanying video directed by Sašo Podgoršek. About Laibach Laibach formed in 1980 in Trbovlje, a mining town in Slovenia, then part of Yugoslavia. The band’s name is the German-language name for Ljubljana, a deliberate reference to the World War II occupation of Slovenia. In December 1984, Laibach co-founded Neue Slowenische Kunst (NSK) alongside the visual-art collective Irwin and the Scipion Nasice Sisters Theatre, uniting music, art and theatre under a single project. The band released its debut album, “Laibach”, in 1985 through the Slovenian label ŠKUC Ropot. From 1987 onward, Laibach recorded primarily for Mute Records, releasing “Krst pod Triglavom – Baptism” and “Opus Dei” in 1987, followed by covers albums “Let It Be” (1988) and “Sympathy for the Devil” (1988/1990). “Kapital” followed in 1992, then “NATO” in 1994, reworking military and pop songs against the backdrop of the Yugoslav wars, and “Jesus Christ Superstars” in 1996, a reinterpretation of the Andrew Lloyd Webber rock opera. “WAT” arrived in 2003, continuing the band’s practice of operating as a collective rather than a fixed lineup. Laibach followed “WAT” with the career-spanning compilation “Anthems” in 2004 and the national-anthem reworking “Volk” in 2006. The band has continued releasing new material into the 2020s, including the symphonic work “Alamut” in 2025 and the studio album “Musick” in 2026.

items.body: Blondie released its third studio album, “Parallel Lines”, on 8 September 1978 through Chrysalis Records. The album turns 48 this year. Mike Chapman produced the record at the Record Plant in New York during June and July 1978, working with the band for the first time after their previous two albums with Richard Gottehrer. Chapman later described the sessions as difficult, recalling Blondie as a band that “didn’t give a fuck about anything” in the studio, while also praising guitarist Frank Infante’s playing. Bassist Nigel Harrison reportedly threw a synthesizer at Chapman during recording out of frustration with his demand for precision. Robert Fripp of King Crimson made a guest guitar appearance on “Fade Away and Radiate”. What is on Blondie’s ‘Parallel Lines’ The album runs 12 tracks: “Hanging on the Telephone” (a cover of The Nerves), “One Way or Another”, “Picture This”, “Fade Away and Radiate”, “Pretty Baby”, “I Know but I Don’t Know”, “11:59”, “Will Anything Happen?”, “Sunday Girl”, “Heart of Glass”, “I’m Gonna Love You Too” (a Buddy Holly cover) and “Just Go Away”. A 2001 remastered reissue added four bonus tracks, and a 30th Anniversary Edition followed on 24 June 2008 with further bonus material and a DVD of promo videos and TV performances. “Picture This”, “I’m Gonna Love You Too”, “Hanging on the Telephone”, “Heart of Glass”, “Sunday Girl” and “One Way or Another” were all released as singles between August 1978 and May 1979. “Heart of Glass” became Blondie’s first US number one on the Billboard Hot 100, and “Sunday Girl” gave the band a UK number one in May 1979. The album itself reached number 1 on the UK Albums Chart in February 1979 and number 6 on the Billboard 200. Edo Bertoglio photographed the cover, chosen by manager Peter Leeds over the band’s own objections. “Parallel Lines” has since been ranked number 140 on Rolling Stone’s list of the 500 greatest albums of all time, and in 2024 was selected for preservation in the US National Recording Registry by the Library of Congress, which cites cultural, historical or aesthetic importance as its selection criteria. About Blondie Blondie formed in New York City in 1974, led by vocalist Debbie Harry and guitarist Chris Stein, growing out of the CBGB and Max’s Kansas City club scene alongside Television and the Ramones. The band released its self-titled debut album in 1976 and “Plastic Letters” in 1977, both produced by Richard Gottehrer, establishing Blondie’s early new wave and punk-adjacent sound. Drummer Clem Burke, keyboardist Jimmy Destri, bassist Nigel Harrison and guitarist Frank Infante joined across these early lineups. “Parallel Lines” in 1978 marked Blondie’s commercial breakthrough, followed by “Eat to the Beat” in 1979 and “Autoamerican” in 1980, the latter carrying the number one singles “Call Me” and “The Tide Is High”. The band broke up in 1982 before reforming in 1997, releasing “No Exit” in 1999 and a string of albums since, including “Pollinator” (2017). The 2022 archival box set “Against the Odds: 1974-1982” was nominated for the Grammy Award for Best Historical Album in 2023. Harry and Stein have remained the band’s constant members across five decades of recording and touring.

items.body: Alphaville released its fifth studio album, “Salvation”, in 1997 through Warner/Metropolis. The album turns 29 this year. Wikipedia lists the release date as 1 September 1997, while MusicBrainz records it as 8 September 1997; Side-Line marks the anniversary on the later date. Andy Richards produced the album for Sarm Productions, recording at Eden Studios in London. The album arrived during a difficult period for the band. Ricky Echolette left Alphaville during production, and Marian Gold and Bernhard Lloyd both later criticised the label’s promotion of the record. “Salvation” was the last Alphaville album on Warner/Metropolis and the last to feature Bernhard Lloyd, who left the band in 2003. What is on Alphaville’s ‘Salvation’ The original 12-track edition runs “Inside Out”, “Monkey in the Moon”, “Guardian Angel”, “Wishful Thinking”, “Flame”, “Point of Know Return”, “Control”, “Dangerous Places”, “Spirit of the Age”, “Soul Messiah”, “New Horizons” and “Pandora’s Lullaby”. The US release added three bonus tracks: “Life Is King”, a “Wishful Thinking” physical mix, and a “Monkey in the Moon” demo. “Wishful Thinking” (February 1997), “Flame” (June 1997) and “Soul Messiah” (1999) were released as singles, though none charted in Germany. Marian Gold sang and played keyboards, Bernhard Lloyd played keyboards and programming, and producer Andy Richards also contributed keyboards and programming. Tim Cransfield played guitars, with Elliott Randall adding electric guitar to “New Horizons”. Anne Dudley arranged strings for “Wishful Thinking” and “Flame”, recorded at Angel Recording Studios; John Altman arranged strings for “Pandora’s Lullaby”. The album returned to the band’s synth-pop roots with a heavier dance and techno influence, drawing comparisons to “Forever Young”. A remastered and expanded deluxe edition followed in November 2023. About Alphaville Alphaville formed in Münster, Germany, in 1982, founded by Marian Gold, Bernhard Lloyd and Frank Mertens; Gold and Lloyd had met in West Berlin the previous year. The band signed to WEA and released its debut album, “Forever Young”, in 1984, carried by the singles “Big in Japan” and “Forever Young”, both international hits. Mertens left the band at the end of 1984 and was replaced by Ricky Echolette (Ricky Olbrich), who remained until 1996. “Afternoons in Utopia” followed in 1986. Alphaville moved toward more experimental territory with “The Breathtaking Blue” (1989) and “Prostitute” (1994) before returning to a more direct synth-pop approach on “Salvation” in 1997. After “Salvation” and Bernhard Lloyd’s 2003 departure, Marian Gold continued Alphaville with a rotating lineup, releasing “Dreamscapes” (1999), “Catching Rays on Giant” (2010) and “Strange Attractor” (2017), alongside a long touring history built around the band’s 1984 hits. Alphaville has remained active into the 2020s, including a 2023 deluxe reissue campaign covering both “Prostitute” and “Salvation”.

items.body: Clan of Xymox released “Farewell” on 8 September 2003 through Metropolis Records in the US. The album turns 23 this year. A Discogs listing for the same US CD pressing shows a street date of 25 August 2003; Metropolis’s own catalogue and MusicBrainz both confirm 8 September as the release date. Ronny Moorings wrote, recorded and mixed the album, co-producing it with Mojca at The Torture Chamber in Amsterdam. Dierk Budde mastered it at Voodoogarden Studio. What is on Clan of Xymox’s ‘Farewell’ The album runs 10 tracks: “Farewell”, “Cold Damp Day”, “There’s No Tomorrow”, “Dark Mood”, “One More Time”, “Into Extremes”, “It’s Not Enough”, “Courageous”, “Losing My Head” and “Skindeep”, with a total running time of just over 59 minutes. Mojca designed the sleeve. The title track received an official video. About Clan of Xymox Clan of Xymox formed in Nijmegen, the Netherlands, in 1981 under the name Xymox, led by Ronny Moorings. The band signed to 4AD and released its debut album, “Clan of Xymox”, in 1985, followed by “Medusa” in 1986, both defining releases in the darkwave and goth rock scene of the period. A move to Polydor and a shortened band name, Xymox, produced “Twist of Shadows” (1989) and “Phoenix” (1991), after which the band’s major-label run ended. Moorings revived the project as Clan of Xymox in 1997, beginning a run of studio albums on Metropolis Records that included “Hidden Faces” (1997), “Notes From The Underground” (2001), “Farewell” (2003) and later albums through the 2000s and 2010s. Side-Line has tracked the band’s catalogue over the years, including Clan of Xymox’s ‘In Love We Trust’ turns 17 on 18 August. Moorings has kept the band active on tour and in the studio into the 2020s, continuing a discography that now spans more than four decades.

items.body: Ultravox, the British new wave and electronic band, released “Systems of Romance” on 8 September 1978 through Island Records. The album turns 48 this year. It was the group’s third studio album, the first credited without the exclamation mark the band had carried since its debut, and the last to feature original singer and lyricist John Foxx. The band recorded it at Conny’s Studio near Cologne, West Germany, with Conny Plank and Dave Hutchins co-producing alongside Ultravox. Guitarist Stevie Shears was dismissed in early March 1978 and replaced by Robin Simon, whose only Ultravox album this is. The line-up was completed by Chris Cross on bass, synthesizer and vocals, Billy Currie on keyboards and violin, and Warren Cann on drums, rhythm machine and vocals. Electronics carried more of the record than on either of the two previous albums: synthesizer bass replaced conventional bass on several tracks, “Quiet Men” used a Roland TR-77 rhythm box in place of drums, and “Dislocation” and “Just for a Moment” dropped acoustic and synthetic drums entirely in favour of treated ARP Odyssey sounds. Cann later described the opening track to interviewer Jonas Warstad as the point where the two halves of the band’s sound met: “it perfectly represented our amalgamation of rock and synthesizer, many of the ideas and aspirations we had for our music gelled in that song”. The ten-track album runs “Slow Motion”, “I Can’t Stay Long”, “Someone Else’s Clothes”, “Blue Light”, “Some of Them”, “Quiet Men”, “Dislocation”, “Maximum Acceleration”, “When You Walk Through Me” and “Just for a Moment”. Island issued “Slow Motion” as a single on 11 August 1978 and “Quiet Men” on 20 October 1978, book-ending the album. The band had already played early versions of both at the Reading Festival on 27 August 1978. Neither single nor the album entered the UK charts. Sales figures differ by source: the 2006 reissue sleeve notes give over 20,000 copies, while Wikipedia’s Ultravox entry cites initial sales of over 25,000. Foxx has explained the title as a borrowing from Plank’s working method and his interest in systems music. “I liked the idea of intangible emotional elements running through mathematical frameworks,” he said. “It seemed a perfect encapsulation of the spirit of the music I was attempting to get to at that moment.” No song of that name appears on the album; Foxx recorded one for his 1981 solo album “The Garden”. British reviews split. In Sounds on 2 September 1978, John Gill rated the album four out of five and wrote: “Whatever anyone says, Ultravox (sans ‘!’) have always been that important step ahead of fashion… Personally I don’t think it’s their best (album) but the deftly alienating production and the tricky use of electronics make it an important enough development in the career of a band that always aims for the unusual”. Island dropped Ultravox on 31 December 1978. The band financed a US tour itself in early 1979, and at its end in March Foxx announced he would leave to work solo, handing the remaining members the band name. He had decided as early as the first Systems of Romance rehearsals, he told Vice in 2013. Simon stayed on in the United States. Currie was recruited that same year by Gary Numan, who has named the 1970s Ultravox as the most important influence on his music, first for a Tubeway Army appearance on The Old Grey Whistle Test and then to play on Gary Numan’s ‘The Pleasure Principle’ and its tour. Cross, Currie and Cann later recruited Midge Ure, who wrote in his 2004 autobiography that he “loved that album”, and whose reconstituted line-up played Systems material live with Ure singing Foxx’s lyrics. About Ultravox Ultravox formed in London in April 1974 as Tiger Lily, on the initiative of Royal College of Art student Dennis Leigh, who later took the name John Foxx. Chris Allen, later Chris Cross, played bass and Stevie Shears guitar; Warren Cann joined on drums in May 1974 and Billy Currie on violin that October. The group released one single as Tiger Lily in 1975 and went through several further names before signing to Island Records in 1976 and settling on Ultravox! in October that year, the exclamation mark a reference to Neu!, another Conny Plank production. Island released the debut “Ultravox!” in February 1977, co-produced by Steve Lillywhite and Brian Eno, and “Ha! Ha! Ha!” later the same year. Neither charted. The closing track of the second album, “Hiroshima Mon Amour”, used a Roland TR-77 drum machine and pointed towards the direction the band took next. “Systems of Romance” moved that balance towards electronics, working with Conny Plank, who had produced Kraftwerk‘s first four albums. After Island dropped the band and Foxx left in 1979, Foxx recorded the electronic solo album “Metamatic” (1980) and then “The Garden” (1981), which revisited the Systems-era material with Robin Simon on guitar; Side-Line covered the complete ‘Cathedral Oceans’ vinyl boxset drawn from his later work in 2016. Cross, Currie and Cann continued with Midge Ure on vocals, guitar and keyboards, signing to Chrysalis Records. “Vienna”, released in July 1980 and again produced by Plank, reached number 3 in the UK on the back of its title single, which peaked at number 2 in early 1981. Ultravox’s ‘Rage in Eden’ followed in 1981, recorded once more at Plank’s studio, then “Quartet” (1982) with George Martin producing, “Lament” (1984) and “U-Vox” (1986). Cann was dismissed before the U-Vox sessions, and the band split after that album’s tour in 1987. Currie reformed Ultravox with new singers for “Revelation” (1993) and “Ingenuity” (1994) before dissolving it again in 1996. Cann, Cross, Currie and Ure reunited in 2008, toured from 2009 and released the studio album “Brilliant” on 28 May 2012; their last show was at London’s O2 Arena on 30 November 2013. Chris Cross died on 25 March 2024, aged 71, as Side-Line reported in Ultravox musician Chris Cross dies aged 71. Chrysalis issued “The Collection (Deluxe Edition)” in December 2025, and Richard Evans published a band biography discussed in Richard Evans on Ultravox. Forty-eight years on, “Systems of Romance” remains the record where the Foxx line-up put its synthesizers at the centre, months before the band that made it came apart.

items.body: In the spring, Eric van Wonterghem returned with a new album from his Monolith project—the sonic alter ego he launched nearly thirty years ago. For the first time, he is releasing a Monolith album on his own label. Yama is the Hindu god of death and justice, responsible for administering justice and punishing sinners; this theme inspired the album’s ten tracks, at least in the digital version. Monolith remains true to the unique and instantly recognizable sound van Wonterghem has cultivated over the years. It is a precise fusion of Tribal rhythms, Industrial sounds, and Trance-like build-ups. The album as a whole—especially the harder tracks—is highly driving and danceable, culminating in a genuine Trance climax. At the same time, calmer, more atmospheric tracks provide welcome variety while still making a distinct impact on the listener. This is largely due to the remarkable atmosphere Monolith creates once again. Another essential element of the project’s signature sound is the Eastern vibe that permeates the tracks and fits the album’s concept perfectly. Eric van Wonterghem remains a true sound guru, particularly when it comes to the icy tones he weaves into his loops. I am also completely captivated by the deep, overwhelming and explosive bass sounds that anchor the tracks and pair perfectly with the driving rhythms. Monolith has never let me down. This Belgian pioneer once more manages to amaze and convince me. In short, another unmissable album. (Rating:8½). Listen to “Shiva”: Shiva by Monolith About Monolith Monolith is the solo project of Belgian musician Eric van Wonterghem, set up in 1997. Van Wonterghem has also worked with Absolute Body Control, The Klinik, Insekt, Sonar, and Detune-X, and has contributed to Dive album productions. The project built its reputation on a Tribal-Industrial sound, a fusion of Tribal percussion, Industrial production, and Trance-style builds that van Wonterghem has continued to refine across more than a decade of releases. In 2016, Monolith released the four-track EP “Time Running Out” (“Construct”, “De-construct”, “Ghost Cities”, and “Time”) on Sonic Groove, later issued on vinyl. The project also runs its own Bandcamp imprint, SoundOfMonolith, used in 2020 to self-release “The Disco Buddha Variations”, new edits of a track van Wonterghem has described as one of his best-known pieces. Van Wonterghem released his eleventh Monolith album, “Unnatural Bodies”, on Hands in 2020, describing the record as an attempt to make “art without rules” inspired by the mechanical-organic sculptures of artist Jim Whiting. He discussed the approach in a 2020 interview with Side-Line. “Yama”, released on van Wonterghem’s own label Prodam Records, is the first Monolith album issued through his own imprint. The digital edition holds ten tracks built around the album’s theme, the Hindu god of death and justice.

items.body: Northern Irish composer Hannah Peel will release her original score for “Underland” on CD on 16 October via Rivertones, followed by a world premiere performance of the score at the Barbican on 24 October as part of the “Hannah Peel: In Focus” two-day series. “Underland” is Peel’s score for Robert Petit’s film adaptation of Robert Macfarlane’s book of the same name. The album combines synthesizers with ancient Mayan pod trumpets and an Iron Age horn called a carnyx, alongside baroque choir and string orchestra. Peel said she read Macfarlane’s book in 2019 and had already used some of its words on her 2022 album “The Unfolding,” calling the chance to score the film itself “beautiful synchronicity.” She described the project as scoring for “these astronauts of the underworld, those sacred ancient cave systems,” and said combining “mythology, technology and possibility” was central to the record. The CD tracklist runs 18 tracks, including “Into the Underland,” “Xibalba,” “Seeing in the Dark,” “The Waiting Wonder,” “You Don’t See Sunlight,” “The Earth Doesn’t Forget,” and “The Ascent.” The Barbican premiere, adapted for stage by Kieran Brunt, will be performed by contemporary vocal ensemble Shards with imagery from the film adapted by director Robert Petit. It forms the second half of “Hannah Peel: In Focus,” which opens on 23 October at Milton Court with “PIA,” a new live production of her 2020 album “Mary Casio: Journey to Cassiopeia,” created with choreographer Katya Bourvis and creative producer Tala Lee-Turton and scored for a 17-piece brass band. The 24 October date also includes a performance of “The Endless Dance,” Peel’s recent album with percussionist Beibei Wang on Real World Recordings. Peel and Beibei Wang will also play the Glasshouse International Centre for Music in Gateshead on 20 October and St Luke’s in Glasgow on 21 October. About Hannah Peel Hannah Peel is a Northern Irish composer, producer, and broadcaster whose work often connects science and music. Her studio albums include “Mary Casio: Journey to Cassiopeia” (2017), scored for synthesizers and colliery brass band; the Mercury Prize-nominated “Fir Wave” (2021); “The Unfolding” (2022) featuring the Paraorchestra; and “The Endless Dance” (2026) with Beibei Wang. Peel received an Emmy nomination for her score on “Game of Thrones: The Last Watch” and has since scored “Scoop” (Netflix), “Bring Them Down” (Mubi), “Midwinter Break” (Focus Features), and the horror film “Saccharine.” Her electronic score for “The Midwich Cuckoos” (Sky) won the Ivor Novello Award for Best Television Soundtrack in 2023, making her the first solo female composer to win that award. Peel also presents BBC Radio 3’s “Night Tracks.” “Underland” continues her run of film and stage work, following its “beautiful synchronicity” with a book she had already drawn on for “The Unfolding.” You Don’t See Sunlight by Hannah Peel

items.body: Emmobiz Records sold a surprise 77-copy marbled vinyl pressing of Apoptygma Berzerk‘s “Kathy’s Song XXV (Come Lie Next to Me)” on September 7, with the entire run gone within 30 minutes. The marbled 12″ was not part of the original announcement. According to Emmobiz, the pressing plant unexpectedly produced the small batch of marbled copies alongside the label’s earlier white and black vinyl editions of the same release, and Emmobiz cleared it for sale once the extra copies turned up. The 77 copies went on sale at 20:00 CEST with a strict one-copy-per-customer limit; orders for more than one copy would have been cancelled entirely. The marbled edition carries the same four tracks as the rest of the “Kathy’s Song XXV” 12″: the Zone Tripper Remix, the 2000 original version, the Mental Overdrive Remix, and the Frak Remix. Side-Line contributor Britta Pirkko already holds one marbled promo copy in her own collection, received ahead of the public sale. It is not for sale. About Apoptygma Berzerk Apoptygma Berzerk is a Norwegian electronic act from Sarpsborg, founded in 1989 by Stephan Groth and Jon Erik Martinsen. Martinsen left early, and Groth has remained the project’s central writer and public face since. “Kathy’s Song (Come Lie Next to Me)” originally appeared on Apoptygma Berzerk’s third album, “Welcome to Earth” (2000), and was issued as its own single via Tatra Records on December 11, 2000. The track has since become one of the project’s best-known songs, marked with a digital 25th-anniversary single in December 2025 and the July 2026 vinyl reissue via Emmobiz that this marbled edition extends. Current members are Stephan Groth, Audun Stengel, Ted Skogmann, and Jonas Groth.

items.body: Irish synthpop project Empire State Human will release a new album, “Opulent,” on CD via ScentAir Records in early 2027. A digital single will arrive ahead of the full album. “Opulent” contains ten tracks written and produced by Aidan Casserly. ScentAir Records is the same label behind Empire State Human’s earlier “Housemuzik” and “ROMO” albums. Casserly wrote and produced the album, with additional production on select tracks from Wave In Head, Sean Barron, and John Giacobello. The album closes with a cover of John Carpenter’s “Halloween,” produced by Casserly. Mastering was handled by Maurizio Pustianaz at Noise Brigade Remasters. The tracklist runs: “Dollar in Blue Collar,” “Vegas Years,” “Strange Star,” “Liquid Blue,” “Film Star,” “Paradise,” “Girl on a Train,” “Halloween,” “The Light,” and “December Rose.” Casserly described “Opulent” as “a very positive, foot tapping and memorable album,” adding that its songs are “sharp” and “at times witty or thoughtful,” with a broad range of themes across the record. He called the sound “romantic electronica” and said he is “looking forward to sharing this album with fans, friends and the scene in 2027.” About Empire State Human Empire State Human is the synthpop project of Irish musician Aidan Casserly. The act built its catalogue through a series of albums for ScentAir Records, including “Housemuzik” and “ROMO,” alongside a 2013 album announcement for “Soul of the Machine” and later output such as the “Legendary” single and the “Robot Love 2002>2009” retrospective compilation. Casserly has also released material outside Empire State Human, including his “Spoken” and “Incubus” albums featuring a rotating cast of collaborators, and the Ferrochrome project with Armageddon Dildos’ Dirk Krause. “Opulent” continues that ScentAir Records partnership, arriving as Empire State Human’s next full-length after a digital single lead-in in the months ahead.

Mixed and mastered by Maurizio Baggio, known for his work with The Soft Moon, Boy Harsher and The Vacant Lots, “Insight” closed out a trilogy that began with the band’s 2016 debut “Observed in a Dream” and continued on 2020’s “Prepared for a Nightmare”. Frontman Trond Fagernes wrote and recorded guitar, bass and vocals over a drum machine first, before adding acoustic drums, synths and guitar contributions from returning founding member Rune Øverby. Insight (Deluxe Version) by Mayflower Madame About Mayflower Madame Mayflower Madame is a post-punk duo from Oslo, Norway, led by Trond Fagernes on vocals, guitar and bass alongside Ola J. Kyrkjeeide on drums. The band debuted with “Observed in a Dream” in 2016, followed by “Prepared for a Nightmare” in 2020, and released “Insight” in November 2024 through Icy Cold Records, Up in Her Room and Night Cult Records. Singles “A Foretold Ecstasy” and “Crippled Crow” carried official videos from that album. The new deluxe vinyl edition of “Insight” extends the record’s life with additional material previously unavailable on the format.

items.body: Purple Trash release their new album “Velvet Nightmares and Cold Sleep” on Swiss Dark Nights. The twelve-track record is out now on digiCD, moving between darkwave, gothic rock, post-punk and electronica. Purple Trash is the solo project of Sergio Da Silva, also known as Bornyhake, a Swiss multi-instrumentalist and composer who has been active on the Swiss underground scene for over twenty-five years and who founded the band Borgne in the 1990s. Da Silva launched Purple Trash in 2020, and “Velvet Nightmares and Cold Sleep” pushes the project deeper into a claustrophobic, self-contained sound, moving between slower, melancholic passages and more electronic, rhythmic territory. Opener “The Echoes of a Sleeping Mind” sets a melancholic tone built around guitar and vocals within its first two minutes, while “Scatterbrain Cathedral” follows with electric guitar and a heavier electronic arrangement. The album’s rhythm section pushes hardest on “It’s a Funeral Pyre”, before “I Tried to Sniff Coffee” returns to a bleaker, more introspective register that runs through the rest of the record. The full tracklist reads “The Echoes of a Sleeping Mind”, “Scatterbrain Cathedral”, “Ashes of Desire”, “I’m Hacking Like a Broke-Down Car”, “Walls Without Names”, “It’s a Funeral Pyre”, “I Tried to Sniff Coffee”, “Chains Made of Gold”, “Through a Forest of Tobacco Trees”, “I Was a Trash Can”, “Feathers in the Shadows” and “A Morning Beyond All Worry”. Velvet Nightmares and Cold Sleep by Purple Trash About Purple Trash Purple Trash is the solo project of Swiss musician Sergio Da Silva, known under the alias Bornyhake, who has been active on the Swiss underground scene for more than twenty-five years. Da Silva founded the band Borgne in the 1990s, entwining ethereal melodies with drum machines. He launched Purple Trash as a solo outlet in 2020, moving between darkwave, gothic rock, post-punk and electronica while keeping the dark, unsettling atmospheres that run through his other work. “Velvet Nightmares and Cold Sleep”, released through Swiss Dark Nights, is his latest album under the Purple Trash name.
