items.body: Golden Apes release their twelfth studio album “The Sun Came Up Tremendously” on Icy Cold Records on 18 September. The ten-track record is out on limited vinyl, digiCD and digital, recorded and produced at Thommy Hein Studios in Berlin. The album continues the Berlin band’s move between post-punk, darkwave and gothic rock, pairing delicate melodies and driving basslines with dense guitar walls, ethereal soundscapes and pulsating drums. The vinyl edition is limited to 300 copies on black vinyl with a lyrics sheet, while the digiCD carries a ten-page lyrics booklet and the exclusive bonus track “City Walls”. The tracklist runs “Farewell”, “The Light (Inside Us)”, “Milk and Poison”, “Resistance”, “Helion”, “Where the River Ran”, “Evelyn (One Day)”, “Radiation” and “Dreams (Gone By)”, with “City Walls” added on CD. Lead single “Resistance” arrived with an official video directed by frontman Peer Lebrecht. Golden Apes tour Germany around the release, playing Moritzbastei in Leipzig on 9 October, Rosenkeller in Jena on 13 November and Privatclub in Berlin on 20 November. Tour dates 9 October 2026 – Moritzbastei, Leipzig (Germany) 13 November 2026 – Rosenkeller, Jena (Germany) 20 November 2026 – Privatclub, Berlin (Germany) About Golden Apes Golden Apes is a post-punk and darkwave band from Berlin, Germany, formed around vocalist and synth player Peer Lebrecht. The band debuted with “Stigma 3.am” in 2000, and released albums including “The Langsyne Litanies” (2014), “MALVS” (2016) and “KASBEK” (2019) before the EP “From the Sky” in 2022 and the album “Our Ashes at the End of the Day” in 2024. The current line-up comprises Lebrecht on vocals and synths, Maximilian Hennig and Stephan Schönefeld on guitars, Christian Lebrecht on bass and Salomon Bosse on drums. The band has played festivals including Wave-Gotik-Treffen and Castle Party, and toured the US, Canada, Russia and Europe. “The Sun Came Up Tremendously” is the band’s twelfth studio album.

items.body: Tout Debord release “Necrologia”, a 32-track double CD compilation, on Icy Cold Records. The digipak gathers the complete collection of EPs and singles the project released between 2021 and 2026, on labels including Detriti Records, Sierpien Records and Salle d’Attente. Tout Debord is the solo project of Leonid Diaghilev, born in Belarus and based in Paris for several years, who wrote, recorded and mixed every song on “Necrologia” himself. The compilation moves from 80s-inspired coldwave to synthpunk influences drawn from the 2000s, filtered through a lo-fi aesthetic across two discs of sixteen tracks each. A vinyl edition with a shorter tracklist is planned for later in the year. About Tout Debord Tout Debord is the solo project of Leonid Diaghilev, a musician born in Belarus and based in Paris, France. The project’s name fuses the French phrase “tout d’abord” (“first of all”) with a nod to philosopher and Situationist Guy Debord. Since starting the project in Paris in 2020, Diaghilev has released a string of EPs and singles across several independent labels, drawing on the early albums of The Cure and industrial synthpop acts such as Fad Gadget and Depeche Mode, alongside the French cold wave scene of the 1980s. “Necrologia”, released through Icy Cold Records, collects that catalogue on a single double-disc release for the first time.

items.body: We were looking forward to being able to talk on the podcast this week about the Diavol Strain set we caught on Sunday, however that won’t be the case. After an apparently awful border crossing into the US the Chilean duo understandably opted not to cross into Canada, as doing so would of course necessitate another entry into the US. Us not getting to see the band behind arguably the year’s best goth record thus far is obviously a drop in the ocean in comparison to larger inconveniences, threats, and acts of violence and murder committed by the current US administration, but it’s a reminder that fascism wants to keep people apart, wants to deny us the opportunity to meet with and learn from those from other parts of the world. You don’t need us to say it, but fuck ICE, fuck white supremacy, fuck everything and everyone related to this atrocity of an American government. Divider Kontravoid, “Without” Oh shit, new Kontravoid incoming. One of the hardest working (and at this point most influential) darkwave acts has been on a tear for a couple of years, with successive banger releases that border on harder industrial, pure synthpop and may other sounds. “Without” continues that trend, with Cam Findlay stretching himself vocally in ways we’ve not yet heard on the new cut, especially on the double-time chorus. Anthemic stuff, and a fine harbinger of what’s to come on October 2nd. Sound of the Void by Kontravoid Dark Chisme, “Suffer Like Me” Seattle’s darkwave duo Dark Chisme has been building their audience the old-fashioned way: by releasing good music, and kicking rich amounts of ass live every time the roll through town. It’s been a real pleasure to watch first hand, especially on their recent show opening up for Omar Doom here in Vancouver where they tore it up on all their established songs, and also tossed this new one “Suffer Like Me” into the mix, which unsurprisingly went over just as well as any other cut they played. Loving the little hints of NRG and freestyle making their way into their sound here, and very keen to hear them continue in this vein in the lead-up to their next album. Suffer Like Me by Dark Chisme Synapscape, “Melting” We’ve had a lot of fun tracking Philipp Münch as he’s dodged down ever odder alleyways over the last few years, from wilfully naive synthpop to oddball dark electro, but a reconvening with Tim Kniep for the project which first brought him international attention is always welcome. Plenty of familiar core elements from across Synapscape’s legacy of powernoise jump out on this teaser from The Future, but the polyrhythmic density which builds up and spirals outward beneath Münch’s restless yowl pushes the envelope quite pleasantly. the future by synapscape Divider, “Nought Point Zero (Portion Control Remix)” Divider’s Zero has been one of the most enjoyable EBM releases of the year, showing how much can be wrought from a little bit of structural experimentation while still holding to no-frills and hard-hitting sound design. Sounds a little like modern day PorCon, no? It’s not surprising, then, to hear how easily a Portion Control bassline can be welded to the moonlit junkyard ambience of the original version of this cut from that record. Nought Point Zero by Divider Silent EM, “Survive (Luminance Remix)” Silent EM isn’t exactly striking while the iron’s hot with a remix LP coming out nearly two full years since the release of Real Life, but a list of contributors including Ortrotasce, Inhalt, Qual, Kontravoid, and Un Hombre Solo brings a lot of star power to this better late than never comp. In particular, the mix of dreamy ghostliness and precise electro pulses on this mix from Brussels-based Luminance is what’s really jumping off the page at us. Silent EM – Real Life (Remixes) by No. Nothing. Never. Records SØLVE, “Nothing Lasts” As is tradition, Brant Showers has released a song on his Birthday as a pay what you want single on Bandcamp. In this case, the song in question is a cover of Matthew Sweet’s “Nothing Lasts”, a classic bit of pop-rock melancholia from the beloved by those who know Girlfriend LP. Far from taking the song into the territory of his usual post-witchhouse ritual dark ambience, Showers plays it straight, amping the spare original into a shoegazey alsice of orchestral pop. Unexpected and absolutely lovely. NOTHING LASTS by SØLVE The post Tracks: September 8th, 2026 appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.excerpt: There is something almost indecent about hearing Soft Cell look backward with this much grace. For a band that once made sleaze, synthetic dread, cheap rooms, lust, humiliation, and metropolitan bad behaviour feel like the natural furniture of pop music, The Rainbow Room finds Marc Almond and Dave Ball staring across Manhattan from 65 floors up and realizing that memory can be every bit as dangerous as desire. items.body: There is something almost indecent about hearing Soft Cell look backward with this much grace. For a band that once made sleaze, synthetic dread, cheap rooms, lust, humiliation, and metropolitan bad behaviour feel like the natural furniture of pop music, The Rainbow Room finds Marc Almond and Dave Ball staring across Manhattan from 65 floors up and realizing that memory can be every bit as dangerous as desire. The song comes from Danceteria, Soft Cell’s sixth and final studio album, completed shortly before Ball’s death in October 2025. It’s set in New York in the early ’80s, when Almond and Ball were recording at Mediasound, running around clubs, meeting Warhol, dancing near Madonna, and absorbing a city seemingly built for people with nowhere respectable to be. The Rainbow Room catches that romance at the point where exhilaration develops a crack. Ball’s arrangement is spacious, elegant, and slightly narcotic. The electronics drift rather than stampede, giving Almond room to sing as though he were paging through photographs nobody else can see. His voice carries wisdom and gravitas; every phrase has the peculiar steadiness of a man who knows how unreliable memory can be yet still chooses to trust it – albeit with rose coloured glasses. This is, in short, Almond’s My Way. The central image comes from Almond’s own birthday visit to Rockefeller Center. “… I did celebrate my birthday – my 21st or 22nd – at The Rainbow Room in the Rockefeller Center… The story of that view is true, too, I really did think: “Imagine falling down there” at the time,” Almond muses. “It was important to mention the Twin Towers, to acknowledge that this song about the future had a poignancy to it, knowing how dark that future would become.” That line about falling is pure Soft Cell: glamour sharing a table with dread, champagne beside the abyss. The Twin Towers turn the song’s future tense into something brutal. Young Almond looks across New York wondering what comes next; older Almond sings from a world in which several answers are already known, including the death of his musical partner. That knowledge changes the record’s emotional gravity. Ball heard the finished album before he passed away, and Almond has said no further Soft Cell recordings are possible without him. The Rainbow Room therefore carries a strange double exposure of youth and aftermath: two men in New York discovering possibility, then those same lives heard decades later through distance, death, and accumulated history. The Rainbow Room takes nostalgia somewhere quieter and more devastating. The city still glitters below, the party is still downstairs, and Almond stands at the window remembering when the future looked endless. Listen below: With the untimely death of Dave Ball in 2025, the band’s sixth and final album, Danceteria, finally arrives on September 25, 2026. You can pre-order Danceteria here. Marc Almond has announced another live run, this time in South America in late November to December. Prior to that, Marc will be playing more European shows in Italy and Poland from late September to October. In early November, Marc returns to the States for a second time this year and will be touring as Soft Cell. The tour begins November 8th in San Diego and includes the Darker Waves festival in California on November 14th. Check out the full listings and ticket links here. Nov 8 San Diego, CA – The Magnolia Nov 10 Napa, CA – Uptown Theatre Nov 11 San Francisco, CA – The Regency Ballroom Nov 13 Reno, NV – Grand Sierra Resort/Casino Nov 14 Huntington Beach, CA – Darker Waves Nov 15 San Luis Obispo, CA – Fremont Theater Follow Soft Cell: Website Instagram Facebook Spotify The post Soft Cell Shares Moving Synthpop Ballad “The Rainbow Room” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: Veronica & the Dark Particles sound as though somebody fed a goth club into a deep-space transmitter, waited for the machine to malfunction, and discovered the malfunction had better bass than the original program. Initial Transmission, the Florida duo’s debut album, comes loaded with retro-futurist synths, rigid post-punk bass, hard electronic percussion, and Veronica Blak’s cool, velvet-toned delivery moving through the machinery with the calm of someone who has already seen the catastrophe beyond the airlock. British composer Eniac Nine gives these eight tracks weight. The bass is thick without turning muddy, the drums land with mechanical discipline, and the synthesizers occupy a wide field that can suddenly feel enormous without losing definition. Blak sits removed from the center of the mix, suited to lyrics preoccupied with obsession, dread, distortion, paralysis, and the queasy suspicion that technology has learned more about us than we have learned about ourselves. “Eniac Nine and I never worked together before but he brought me such a compelling collection of diverse tracks that the lyrics and melodies formed almost instantly in my head,” says Blak. “I like the unique sounds he crafts for each song like a spaceship door opening in Digital or Indian tabla inspired drums on Monster that you don’t hear in modern darkwave.” Liquify begins with an electronic throb that feels clinical, almost chemical, its bass moving with the slow certainty of something spreading through the bloodstream. Small synthetic details hover around the beat while Blak’s voice supplies the human temperature, cool and controlled even as the arrangement grows more claustrophobic. Digital is stranger and more playful, crawling forward on a crooked, slinky rhythm that recalls Strange Boutique launched several thousand miles beyond Earth. Synthetic noises open and close around the song like mechanical doors, giving its groove the peculiar sensation of wandering through some abandoned pleasure station where the computers have kept the music running after the passengers disappeared. Monster throws subtlety aside for speed and impact, propelled by tabla-inspired percussion, hard electronic drums, and one of the album’s biggest hooks. Blak rides above the commotion with enough authority to make the chorus feel ready for collective shouting in a packed club. Rumors lowers the temperature and gives anxiety room to multiply. Its slower movement produces a particular kind of paranoia, where every empty measure seems capable of concealing another piece of bad information. The scale feels enormous without sacrificing intimacy, turning private suspicion into something closer to societal collapse viewed through a bedroom window. Dunes ventures much farther outside conventional darkwave coordinates. Strange synthetic tones, threatening low frequencies, and a cinematic sense of distance suggest some hostile future civilization whose architecture was designed without human comfort in mind. Lost retreats into more recognizably European coldwave territory, recalling Clan of Xymox and Lebanon Hanover through its severe bass movement and unusual pockets of echo. Voices and instruments seem displaced from one another, as though the song were being heard simultaneously from several adjoining rooms. Then comes The Kiss, their treatment of The Cure’s 1987 classic, trimmed into a tighter form with an unexpectedly sharp pop instinct. Robert Smith’s original recording sprawls through obsession until guitar becomes nearly physical pressure; Veronica & the Dark Particles concentrate that fever into a more economical attack. The bass carries much of the psychological weight, while Blak approaches the lyric with a colder sensuality that makes its possessiveness feel calculated rather than delirious. Closing track Rings widens everything again, bringing broad synthesizer passages and space-rock scale into the album’s final stretch. After seven songs spent probing machines, desire, fear, and psychological contamination, the record ends staring outward into an expanse too large to explain, sending its final signal into whatever might be listening. Listen to Initial Transmission below and order the album here. Initial Transmission by Veronica & the Dark Particles “I don’t like single sounds, I like to mix things together to intentionally create complex layers like stacking monosyths,” says Nine. “I write music almost daily, visualizing the texture of sound like a wave table. I don’t rely on samples or loops because I am compelled to craft a universe of unique elements.” That philosophy explains why Initial Transmission works best when its surfaces collide: club music with gothic reserve, machine order with psychological unease, elegance with menace. Veronica & the Dark Particles have made a debut built for black rooms, highway drives after midnight, and the uneasy pleasure of dancing while the future looks increasingly untrustworthy. items.body: The mind protects itself by hiding what it cannot yet bear to see. Trauma may become a locked room whose very door triggers fear. Denial, dissociation, and avoidance are not proof of hidden programming, but ways consciousness narrows around pain until, with safety, the forbidden room can be approached again. Planeswalkers begin their odyssey with an unusually literal name. The collaboration between gothic songstress Arden Leigh and electronic composer Andrew Means takes its title from the occult idea of moving consciousness between planes through dreams, trance, meditation, astral projection, or other altered states. Their debut EP, The Mind Room, turns that metaphysical vocabulary toward trauma, dissociation, memory, and recovery, imagining the psyche as a series of sealed chambers approached indirectly when direct confrontation feels overwhelming. The record’s premise draws on Leigh’s belief that extreme trauma can create psychological “tripwires,” while denial and avoidance may become forms of protection. Such language carries obvious clinical and spiritual complications, yet The Mind Room is most persuasive when it translates those ideas into texture and movement rather than explanation. Leigh describes the partnership in explicitly occult terms: “Andrew is a really skilled psychic, one of the best I’ve ever met, and he predicted that we’d have more success with it this way. I got a third-party divination just to be sure, and sure enough, it said he was right. We decided to name ourselves Planeswalkers after our shared occult hobbies…I’d say Andrew is a lot better at planeswalking than I am, but I get the job done when needed, or I compensate for it with other aspects of my practice. There were times when we’d finish working on music and then lie down on my floor and astral project together. It’s a really amazing gift to have met someone who shares my two main interests of music and magick like that, and I’m really looking forward to seeing how we continue to explore both of them as we keep working together.” Across four tracks, The Mind Room treats psychic exploration as both subject and compositional principle. The rooms keep changing shape, and the record’s deepest question remains simple: how does someone approach what the mind has placed behind a locked door? Horizons opens amid static, distant electronics, and gentle cymbals. Leigh’s voice floats high above the arrangement with an Enya-like purity, making the track resemble a guided meditation intercepted by an unstable transmission. Its spacious trip-hop architecture recalls Massive Attack, though ruptures of noise repeatedly disturb the calm. Clockwork gives the EP firmer physical dimensions. Leigh’s commanding register suggests Zola Jesus, while Means bends electronic tones into an uncanny interior where corridors seem to extend past their logical endpoints. Repetition becomes claustrophobic, and the title begins to feel mechanical in the psychological sense: a mind caught inside patterns that continue moving after conscious control has weakened. Body makes the sharpest turn. Trip-hop drums support a leering chant, voices push toward shouting, and the earlier inward drift acquires force. The lyric about “walking the planes” supplies the duo with their name, but the song remains intensely corporeal, concerned with breath, rhythm, threat, and will. The closing Alive returns to open space and echo, with Leigh’s voice receding and reappearing as though consciousness were adjusting to gravity after an excursion elsewhere. Order The Mind Room here and listen below: “For resources on plurality, including traumagenic DID, or to make a donation, we recommend supporting The Plural Association here,” suggest the band. Follow Planeswalkers: Instagram YouTube The post Gothic Electronic Duo Planeswalkers Unlock the Psyche on Debut EP “The Mind Room” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.

items.body: Dungeon synth, the offspring of '90s black metal and ambient music, is a lo-fi genre with a focus on fantastical settings and sonic themes. Ambient music is exactly how it sounds and needs no in-depth explanation for music enthusiasts, and the same attitude extends to the 1990s concrete wave of black metal. Comfy synth, one of numerous prefix-synth sister genres, concentrates on sentimentality and nostalgic sounds; a comfy atmosphere with finite overlap with metal. Comfy synth is a relatively new style, rising in the late 2010s—arguably with Grandma's Cottage's self-titled record, released in December 2019—while dungeon synth falls many decades back. The man behind Hole Dweller, Tim Rowland is a true synth pioneer. Situated in Atlanta, he brought dungeon-infused comfy synth to the ([extremely] relative) mainstream with 2019's Flies the Coop, completing a trilogy started in 2024. His most recent album, Long Road Home, caught my eye this week—mostly through the album art, but partially because of the online hubbub surrounding it. At a digestible half-hour runtime, it isn't a daunting introduction to the genre. Each of the fourteen tracks spans no longer than two minutes (the longest, "stay while the birds sing," reaches 2:47, while "painted in memory" only runs to 1:33), and this is on purpose: Rowland focuses on minimalism, and each track can be looped, like video game soundtracks. Other instruments, like a stringed folk guitar of sorts, are welcome, frequenting tracks with rain and/or nature sounds. The darkest highlight is "bones consumed by moss and root," which takes a badass title and turns the mood to melancholic instead of hopeful. That being said, there are some instances where the focus is taken slightly away from the pure ambience that Hole Dweller convinced me to love in just one playthrough. One is the soft percussion in "summer inventory," and while a steady beat isn't an awful inclusion, the song following it, "sleeping fields," exemplifies that soft cinematics are better on their own, and "in the afterglow" follows this trend. The only other gripe I have is the shift from lo-fi to modern production means. The LP's overall quality dips during "grace in low places" and "in the afterglow", and—despite it being in dungeon synth's nature to not sound crystal clear—the bulk of Long Road Home seems very present-day. This isn't even a complaint though, really, since this duality of feels is perfect for introductory dungeon synthers. Personally, I need no further convincing to join Hole Dweller on the Long Road Home. Long Road Home by Hole Dweller

items.body: 会期：2026/06/26〜2026/06/28 会場：新宿2丁目・こった創作空間［東京都］ 脚本・演出・音楽：外崎銀河 公式サイト：https://www.instagram.com/p/DXHBNnJkotF/ 「クィア当事者の視点から、クィア演劇を創作する」。そんな言葉を掲げ、劇団「薔薇族」がミュージカル『薔薇族’70』でその活動をスタートした。作品タイトルのみならず劇団名にもなっている「薔薇族」とは、かつて存在した1971年に創刊され2004年まで定期刊行されていたゲイ雑誌の名前だ。そこから転じてゲイを意味するものとしても使われるようになったこの言葉を作品タイトルのみならず劇団名として掲げたのは、かつて英語圏において侮蔑語として使われていたクィアという言葉が当事者によって自らの存在を肯定する言葉として使われるようになっていったのと同じように、「薔薇族」という言葉もそうなっていってほしいという願いからなのだという。背景にはもちろん、日本の演劇界には未だに、クィア当事者であることをオープンにして活動しているつくり手が数えるほどしかいない現状と、それに対する問題意識がある。演劇界にも当たり前に存在しているはずのクィア当事者を可視化し、未だに誤解や偏見も多いクィア表象を、まずは当事者の手に取り戻すこと。 劇団「薔薇族」を立ち上げ、『薔薇族’70』の脚本・演出・音楽をひとりで手がけたシンガーソングライターの外崎銀河はしかし、2000年生まれの若き作り手であり、『薔薇族』の世代ではない。それどころか外崎は、2025年11月末に『94歳のゲイ』という映画を見て初めて雑誌『薔薇族』のことを知ったのだという。雑誌『薔薇族』の存在にインスパイアされた外崎はそれからわずか7カ月後に『薔薇族’70』を上演することになる。2026年6月のプライドマンスに、ゲイタウンとして知られる新宿二丁目のスペースで上演されたこの作品のタイトルと劇団名には、未だに婚姻の平等も包括的差別禁止法も実現していない日本を生きてきた先人たちへのリスペクトと、その営みを継承し前に進めようという決意が込められている。 ［撮影：高橋明大］ ミュージカル『薔薇族’70』は、かつてマッチングアプリもインターネットもない時代に同性愛者や両性愛者らの交流において大きな役割を果たしていた『薔薇族』の文通欄とそこから生まれる交流を軸に物語を展開していく。時は1971年。主な登場人物は6人。成長するにつれて失われていく自らの美しさを嘆き、虚空に言葉を吐き出すように文通欄に投稿する「美少年」（遠藤光基）。書店でたまたま『薔薇族』を目にしたことをきっかけに、自らの男性に対する気持ちを改めて思い出すことになる「夫」（水越とものり）。自らが男性同性愛者であることを受け入れ、生きたいように生きると嘯く「同性愛者」（樋口祥久）。まだ見ぬ出会いを求めて投稿を繰り返す「役者」（丸山真矢）。その役者と文通欄を介して出会い、関係を深めていく「独身男性」（谷怜由）。そして「夫」が男と文通を重ねている事実に気づくことになる「妻」（新田絢加）。加えて物語を枠づけ過去を現代とつなぐ「ストーリーテラー」を外崎自身が演じていた。 ［撮影：高橋明大］ 「夫」のように自身が同性愛者であることから目を逸らしながら、あるいはそれを隠しながら結婚をし、家庭を築き、子供まで設けるような生き方は、現在の視点から見れば大いに問題があるように思える。だが、その背景には男性の生涯未婚率が1〜2%ほどに留まっていた当時の状況がある。皆婚社会と名指された当時においては、結婚をしないという選択肢はそもそもほとんど考慮の埒外にあったのだ。その意味では、我が道を行くことを堂々と宣言する「同性愛者」は例外的な存在であり、「夫」と対になるような存在だと言えるだろう。二人は文通を通じて交流を深めるが、それに気づいた「妻」の介入でその出会いは実現せず、二人の道は再びすれ違う。そして「夫」と「妻」は何事もなかったかのようにこれまでの生活を続けていくことを誓い合うだろう。 だが、より若い世代には現在にも通じる希望が託されている。実は「夫」と「妻」の息子でもあった（！）「独身男性」は両親の間に起きたことを知り、母をこれ以上悲しませたくないと「役者」に別れを切り出す。しかし死ぬのでなければ結婚するしかないと思い詰める「独身男性」の辿る道は両親の辿ったそれと重なるものだろう。二人は一度は別れを受け入れるものの、やがて固く手をつなぎ舞台を去っていく。 ［撮影：高橋明大］ 一方、そんな二人に現実を突きつけようとするかのように「美少年」は独白する。「やっぱり全て、うまくいかないと思うんです。僕たちは世の中に否定されてるわけだし、誰にも応援されない。一生孤独で、一生寂しいまま、死ぬんです。（中略）このまま生きていたって、歳をとって醜くなるだけ。それだったら今…」。しかしそんな「美少年」のもとに思わぬ手紙が届く。それはなんと「妻」からの手紙だ。「夫」が男と浮気をしていたことが許せないと語る妻は同時に、夫を愛しているからこそ、夫がそのような生き方を選ばざるを得ないこの社会のことが許せないのだと言う。「妻」は語りかける。苦しんでいるのはあなただけではない。そしてまだ若いあなたは、変わっていく世の中を楽しむことが、社会を変えていくことができるはずだと。「妻」の言葉には、外崎が『薔薇族』や上の世代から受け取ったものや、そこから芽吹いた決意が込められてもいるだろう。 ［撮影：高橋明大］ ［撮影：高橋明大］ ミュージカルという形式は文通欄への投稿と手紙のやりとりを軸にしたこの作品によくマッチしていた。誰にともなく差し出される言葉と交差する複数の手紙のやりとり。それらを通じて登場人物の感情がときに交わり、すれ違い、あるいは寄り添い響き合う様が音楽の構造と力を借りて立体的に立ち上がっていたのだ。 一方、作品全体としては課題も多かったように思う。物語の面ではやはり「妻」の描き方には問題があると言わざるを得ない。夫と息子の両方が同性愛者だったというご都合主義な（？）展開には目をつぶるにしても、次世代の同性愛者に希望を託す役割を担わされた「妻」の生が、同性愛者との関わりにおいてしか描かれていなかった点はいただけない。「妻」の生もまたひとりの個人としての奥行きのあるものであるはずだが（同性愛者のそれと同じように！）、残念ながらそのことが十分に描かれているとはいえない。これでは同性愛者にとって（そして作品にとって）都合のいい存在として「妻」を利用したと言われても仕方ないだろう。 また、商業ミュージカルでも活躍する俳優らはさすがの歌唱力で魅せたものの、4メートル四方の舞台で最大6人もの俳優が出入りしながら、しかも複数の時空間を行き来する構成は、上演としてはあまりにごちゃごちゃして見えた。劇団の旗揚げを新宿二丁目で、という思いは理解できるものの、あの空間であれば今回はリーディング公演のような設えでもよかったのではないだろうか。基本的にはこれらは演出の問題であり、音楽畑出身の外崎にとっては最大の課題と言えるかもしれない。 とはいえ、劇団「薔薇族」が志ある、そして残念ながら2026年の日本においては稀有な存在であることは間違いない。その旗揚げを改めて祝福したい。劇団「薔薇族」としては9月25日（金）に南青山MANDALAで行なわれる外崎銀河のワンマンライブ内で一人（？）ミュージカル『ゲAI』を上演予定とのこと。 ［撮影：高橋明大］ 観賞日：2026/06/26（金）

items.excerpt: 会期：2026/07/11～2026/07/12 会場：三重県文化会館 小ホール［三重県］ 公式サイト：https://hatetocheek.com/kimitomo2026/ 「しんどいのはみんな同じ」という言葉が「共感」「慰め」の形を借りて発せられるとき、なぜ、何が問題なのか。社会構造や規範、他者からの一方的なジャッジがもたらす抑圧の経験が「それぞれ異なる」という差異自体が覆い隠され、「ないこと」にされてしまうからだ。とりわけこの言葉がマジョリティからマイノリティに向けて発せられるとき、互いに「ともだち」と思っている関係には、わかりあえなさの深い断絶が口を開ける。だが、マジョリティ／マイノリティの構造自体も絶対的で固定的なものではなく、状況によって流動的に揺らぎ、勾配が変動し、あるいは多層的に重なり合っている。「喫煙なんて、将来の赤ちゃんのために良くない」という「善意の心配」がはらむ、「女性は当然、出産するべき」というジェンダー規範。社会に空気のように浸透し、洗い流そうとしてもこびりついたシスヘテロ規範や無意識の偏見に基づくマイクロアグレッション、「言い方が大げさだ」と非難の矛先
items.body: 会期：2026/07/11～2026/07/12 会場：三重県文化会館 小ホール［三重県］ 公式サイト：https://hatetocheek.com/kimitomo2026/ 「しんどいのはみんな同じ」という言葉が「共感」「慰め」の形を借りて発せられるとき、なぜ、何が問題なのか。社会構造や規範、他者からの一方的なジャッジがもたらす抑圧の経験が「それぞれ異なる」という差異自体が覆い隠され、「ないこと」にされてしまうからだ。とりわけこの言葉がマジョリティからマイノリティに向けて発せられるとき、互いに「ともだち」と思っている関係には、わかりあえなさの深い断絶が口を開ける。だが、マジョリティ／マイノリティの構造自体も絶対的で固定的なものではなく、状況によって流動的に揺らぎ、勾配が変動し、あるいは多層的に重なり合っている。「喫煙なんて、将来の赤ちゃんのために良くない」という「善意の心配」がはらむ、「女性は当然、出産するべき」というジェンダー規範。社会に空気のように浸透し、洗い流そうとしてもこびりついたシスヘテロ規範や無意識の偏見に基づくマイクロアグレッション、「言い方が大げさだ」と非難の矛先を巧妙にすり替えるトーンポリシング、そしてセクシュアル・マイノリティが日常の端々で直面する困難を、本作はテンポのよい会話劇で解像度を上げてあぶり出していく。2025年の初演後、東京と三重で再演された。 ［撮影：水澤桃花］ 舞台は、地下にある寂れたカラオケ店。上手に受付カウンター、中央にカラオケルーム、下手に公衆電話ボックスのような一人用の喫煙ブースが設置されている。階段を降りながら、ナンパ目的でしつこく声をかけてくる男に罵声を浴びせるノンバイナリーの野澤。高校の同級生・由海の結婚式の途中、野澤のパートナーのノリちゃんが気分が悪くなり、付き添いとして途中退出したため、カラオケ店で飲み直すことにしたという。そこに、幼馴染の園（その）と、園の恋人で同じ会社の先輩でもある甲斐田が合流する。カラオケ店は、野澤と園の大学時代の友人・衛の親が経営し、衛はアルバイトをしながら音楽活動を続けている。 ［撮影：水澤桃花］ 久しぶりに会った野澤、園、衛の3人と、野澤と衛とは初対面の甲斐田。アルコールの力も借りた空元気と気まずさが同居する二次会は、近況報告の会話のなかに、トランスジェンダー女性であるノリちゃんが直面するさまざまな困難を浮かび上がらせていく。ノリちゃんが結婚式で吐いてしまったのは、新婦の由海が「すべての恋人に幸せを」と言って野澤たちにブーケを手渡したからだ。「色んな愛の形がある」とスピーチしてブーケトスした由海は、園の目には感動的に映るが、「多様な性を認めて祝福しよう」という由海の言動は、自らが異性愛というマジョリティ側にいるという自覚に欠けており、善意で発せられたものであるからこそ野澤とノリちゃんを傷つけてしまう。 だが、もともと体調が良くなかったノリちゃんが吐いてしまった理由は、ブーケトスだけではなかった。前の職場では、「ありのままの姿を応援します！」というコピーとともに自社広告に載せられ、ダイバーシティ推進の広告塔にされかけていた。そして、LGBTQフレンドリーを掲げる（ただしHPに掲載されているのはほぼゲイの経験談である）転職先の会社に希望を見出すも、採用担当者から「女子トイレは使わないで」と真っ先に言われ、そのことをSNSに投稿したら炎上してしまい、リストカットを繰り返す精神的に不安定な状態に追い込まれていた。 ノリちゃんが不在の場で、さらに野澤を追い詰めるのが、甲斐田からの「相談」だ。なんと、ノリちゃんの転職先は園と甲斐田の会社であり、甲斐田はノリちゃんの上司候補だと明かされる。「どう対応したらよいか」とアドバイスを求める甲斐田は一見誠実だが、彼自身、トランス女性とトランス男性の違いもわからず、基礎的な知識すらない。野澤は混乱してうろたえながらも、「でもめちゃくちゃ特別な人間てわけじゃないんですよ」「一人一人違うので、どこまで許容できるかみたいなことが」「ノリちゃんは、やっぱり男性としては扱ってほしくない、というか、だからあの、それだけだとは思うんですよ、基本的には」と説明する。だが、「俺らは良いんだけど、社員の、まあ女性が」と言う甲斐田の周囲には、トランスフォビアがまとわりついている。 ［撮影：水澤桃花］ 園もまた、ノリちゃんのことを快く思っておらず、「佐川さん」とよそよそしく苗字で呼び、それを察している野澤も園にはノリちゃんを会わせていない。トランス女性に対して園が抱く嫌悪感は、もう一人の高校時代の友人、まーちゃんについてのエピソードで示される。美大に進んだまーちゃんは、アート界の不均衡なジェンダーバランスや（おそらくそれに基づく）性被害に遭い、SNSでトランス女性排除に回ってしまった。だが、園は「あんだけ男からクソみたいな目にあったら、男の体で？ みたいな、受け入れられないのもわかるけどね」と発言する。園も元彼から暴力を振るわれた経験がある。だが園には、トランス女性が日常的に直面する偏見や困難に加えて、（トランスフォビアと女性蔑視という二重の負荷によって）トランス女性も・性的嫌がらせの対象になりうる事態がまったく見えていない。 価値観の齟齬や深い断絶は、園と甲斐田という異性愛のカップルの間にも存在する。「結婚しても子どもは欲しくない」と言う園に対し、「結婚したら当然子どもをもつべき」「子どものいる家庭＝幸せ」という価値観に何の疑問ももたない甲斐田との仲は、ギクシャクときしみ始める。また、本作は、男性どうしの格差やマイクロアグレッション、男性社会の抑圧もすくい上げて描写する。甲斐田と衛の間には正社員／アルバイトという格差があり、「音楽で成功できず、パラサイトシングルで、甲斐田のように結婚して子どもをもつ未来図など描けない」というコンプレックスを衛は抱えている。だが、男性性の規範を体現したような甲斐田自身、親兄弟や会社に染みついたホモソーシャルな空気に否応なく飲み込まれていることに、恐怖と息苦しさを感じていることが吐露される。 それぞれの人間関係の軋轢や抑圧が増幅され、蓄積されて臨界点を迎え、衛が甲斐田に水をぶっかけるという突発的な暴力の形で噴き出す。園は「野澤も佐川さんも大変だと思うけど、でも大変なのは皆同じじゃん」と諌めるが、野澤は「あたしとあんたのしんどさは、違うんじゃない？」と指摘する。採用担当者との相談の日、ノリちゃんはトイレのことを言われても、泣いたり怒ったりせず、「普通」に見えたと甲斐田は言う。だが、「その“普通”でいるために、あの日ノリちゃんがどれだけ努力したかっていうのは、分かりますか？」と野澤は尋ねる。「人間なんです、あたしも、だから一生懸命、どうしたらここで受け入れてもらえるかってずっと考えてるんですよ」と。「その、頑張ってきた全部、を、皆同じとか、しんどいとか、そんな、そんな言葉で、あんたがナシにしないで、お願い」──野澤の言葉は、園が「ともだち」と思っているからこそ深く突き刺さる。そして、「……よかったよ、あんたがそっち側で」「そっちは眺める側だから、見なくて済んでよかったよ」と園に向けられる痛烈な皮肉は、「演劇の舞台」という構造とも重ねられ、「マイノリティの物語を安全な距離から一方的に眺め、消費する観客」に対しても向けられるものだろう。 「もうやめよう。おしまいにしよう」という野澤の台詞は、「噛み合わず、徒労に終わるだけの会話はもうやめよう」という文字通りの意味の裏に、「園との友人関係の破綻」を示唆する。それぞれ野澤と園を演じる升味加耀と川村瑞樹が共同主宰するユニット「果てとチーク」の名前は、「hate to hope」に由来し、この2つの単語を英語で読むと「ヘイト」と「希望」という正反対の意味が浮かび上がる。「果てとほっぺ（頬）」というローマ字読みと、「ヘイトと希望」という英単語の二重の意味を、異なる角度から同時に読むことは可能か。「ヘイト」の只中に「希望」はどう見出せるのか。言葉遊びの駆使のなかに、切実な希求が込められている。 ［撮影：水澤桃花］ 後編では、こうしたダブルミーニングを念頭に置きつつ、野澤と園をめぐる終盤の展開を見ていく。ここには、「傷を再び反復しない形でどうやって語ることができるのか」というマイノリティが抱えるジレンマと根本的な問題が横たわっている。また、「劇中、なぜノリちゃんは不在化されているのか」という問いに焦点を当てるとともに、「カラオケボックス」という設定の秀逸さと、「個室の喫煙ブース」という装置の両義性についても掘り下げる。 items.body: For a few years, I have had this funny vision of Antwerp’s Summer Bummer festival taking place on a beach near a body of water. I had sunshine, seagull calls and good vibes in this fantasy. In reality, the venue, a rock club called Trix, is located on a busy road amongst high-rise apartment buildings just outside of downtown Antwerp. So, no seagulls, no beach and even the sun was being fickle. It troubled me, what could be the source for this misconception? The only part I had right was the ‘good vibes’. From the moment the first band started up in the darkened main hall on Friday afternoon to the closing tones of a bass-clarinet and electronics show on the intimate cafe stage late Saturday night, there was always something to hear, records to dig, people to talk shop with, and art to make — hardly leaving time to lament the waning days of the summer. Within the compact time-frame, starting late afternoon and ending around midnight on Friday and Saturday, festival organizers Koen Vandenhout and Christel Kumpen ran a tight program. Concerts were lined-up one after the other with a short break built-in to give the 200+ audience a chance to eat some dinner without developing FOMO. Plus, the sets ping-ponged from the main hall side to the cafe side, so there was always a chance to hit the bar if desired. Between the two halls, merch tables were arranged on all sides, making it dangerous to the wallet to traverse the venue. Parent organization of the festival Sound in Motion’s own Dropa-Disc label was present, as well as a record dealer with a selection of rare taste and local radio station Radio Centraal. If one purchased a t-shirt, or happened to have an extra one on hand, he or she (more likely than not: he) could head into the screen printing workshop and make their own with a festival design. Additionally, set in an adjacent room, musicians Cath Roberts and Tullis Rennie invited festival goers to record and manipulate sounds in a laboratory of their own design. When the weather was cooperative, one could visit the courtyard to procure some homemade food. Alexander von Schlippenbach and Paal Nilssen-Love The Sound In Motion website has the tagline, “Adventurous Music and Things”, and since we have got the things part out of the way, let us talk adventurous music . Not just a free-jazz festival, Summer Bummer’s scope this year included several avant-noise and electronics acts along with some of the most exciting musicians working (primarily) in Europe today. There was something for everyone, for example the ear-bleedingly loud Integral , a quartet comprised of Julien Desprez (guitar), Claire Gapenne (electronics and vocals), Christine Abelnour (sax) and Lukas Koenig (drums) that went from beguiling to battering, to the opening act, Kabas Sun Dogs, a Belgian band who had invited Canadian saxophonist Karen Ng and guitarist Jonathan Horne for a slowly unfolding exploration of both understatement and spirited groove. Rodrigo Amado, Joelle Leandre and Gerald Cleaver Highlights festooned the program, including a first time duo of drummer Paal Nilssen-Love and the legendary pianist Alexander von Schlippenbach as well as new trio formed by Rodrigo Amado with bassist Joelle Leandre and drummer Gerald Cleaver . In the duo’s extended set, Schlippenbach performed a chain of melodic ideas and Thelonius Monk song snippets that Nilssen-Love challenged with closely attuned force and precision. After a cautious opening, the trio of Amado, Leandre and Cleaver edged their way into the set, gathering momentum to the findcommon ground, letting Amado release his powerful tenor, Leandre impress with speed and expressiveness, and Cleaver move seamlessly between texture and forceful pulse. Daughter, Daughter The formidable quartet of Daughter, Daughter, comprised of Camila Nebbia and Amalie Dahl (saxophones), Elizabeth Coudoux (cello) and Sun Mi Hong (drums), performed a blend of composition and free-jazz improvisation showcasing both individual contributions as well as whole group interactions. The Berlin formation Das B , featuring Mazen Kerbaj (trumpet), Magda Mayas (piano), Tony Buck (drums) and Mike Majkowski (bass) was given the designation as a “super group“ in the program and their set did not refute this. Ostensibly deconstructing John Coltrane’s A Love Supreme , the quartet engaged in an exploratory and expansive sound collage complete with a trumpet played via surgical tubing and prepared piano that made the acoustic sound electric. Arguably one of the strongest shows of the festival. Das B Additionally, percussionist and singer Maria Portugal presented her EROSÃO Septet (Lotte Anker and Angelika Niescier on saxes , Matthias M üller and Moritz Wesp on trombones , Carl Ludwig H übsch on tuba and Reza Askari on bass ) , which performed a set of mid-tempo songs, both self-penned and from Brazilian composers, laced with some spicy improvisations. The next day, Portugal appeared in an exceptional duo with pianist Marta Warelis . As opposed to the septet, in which the music was a presented in more traditional structures, the songs themselves were de-composed and integrated organically with the ideas flowing from the pianist whose gentle and spacious playing grew progressively more ferocious. Marta Warelis and Maria Portugal Rounding out the program were two bass clarinet focused sets and several quite noisy ones. Representing the louder side, in addition to the aforementioned Integral, were New Best Friends (featuring Ng and Horne along with bassist Aaron Lumley and drummer Nasim L-P Navarro), the duo of Laurentiu Cotac and Diana Miron, and Mopcut with Desprez, Koenig and electronicist/vocalist Audrey Chen. Of these three, New Best Friends balanced their clamorous impulses best with a flowing set of improvisations. Bookending the festival were two bass clarinet sets. On the first day, John McCowen explored the extended tonalities of the acoustic contra-bass clarinet, exploiting the instrument’s multiphonic capabilities. Closing the festival, Hanna De Backer , in collaboration with the electronics of Yves De Mey , extended her instrument’s sonic possibilities to the outer realms. Overall, a musically adventurous and enjoyable festival, and although quite satisfied, I was still bothered by one thing: my imaginary festival on a beach. So, after some detective work, I believe I finally pinpointed the source of my whimsical misconception. In 2019, Rodrigo Amado's The Attic released the album Summer Bummer , recorded at the festival in 2018 and whose cover is an image of three cut-out figures sitting on a beach under a cloudless blue sky, looking out at the ocean. I didn’t know I was so impressionable! Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: 目次 京都のロック無頼派、FRYING DUTCHMANが14年ぶりの新作を完成!! 言葉とリズムで愉快に真理を突くFRYING DUTCHMANのディスコグラフィー 京都のロック無頼派、FRYING DUTCHMANが14年ぶりの新作を完成!! 京都を拠点に活動する3人組バンド、FRYING DUTCHMAN。ブルースやロックンロールのエッセンスを濃縮した音世界を形成したのは、バンドの中心人物であるLEE TABASCO（ヴォーカル／ギター）が生まれ育った京都の風土とジャンルレスな音楽的土壌であった。 「生まれ育ったのはバリバリの下町。いまは再開発でだいぶ変わったけど、京都でいちばん柄の悪いところでした。京都は若い人から重鎮まで、個性的な人が多いんですよ。変態的な人というか。FRYING DUTCHMANを始めた2000年代前半はまだロック・バンドやブルース・バンドもぎょうさんおったし、あちこちでセッションが行われてました。でも、いまはロック・バンドやセッションしていたお店もほとんどなくなりましたね。オリジナル・メンバーだったベーシストの麻男がサイケ・トランスのDJもやってたので、僕らもよくサイケのイヴェントに遊びに行って、そこでライヴもしてました。サイケの流れで出会ったプロデューサー兼パーカッショニスト／ヴォーカリストの野毛乱もバンドに加わり、そういったメンバーでファースト・アルバム『I WANNA GO OUT』を録りました」。 FRYING DUTCHMANでの活動と並行して、LEEはたびたび世界各地を放浪。国内外での奔放な活動からバンドはカルト的な支持を集めるようになっていく。そんなFRYING DUTCHMANの名を広く知らしめたのが、福島第一原子力発電所事故以降の混沌とした世情への想いをメッセージに乗せた“humanERROR”（2011年）だった。 「あの事故から1か月後に、ぶわっと出てきた言葉をそのまま曲にしたのが“humanERROR”やったんですよ。案の定、恐ろしいほどの反響がありました。でも、あの曲は20～30分かけて本気の怒りを全開で放出するから、歌うほうは怒りを持ち続けないといけなくて、すごく負荷がかかるんです。4、5年ほど全国を回ってやり続けていたら内臓が壊れてしまって。曲の最後に愛がなければもっと早くぶっ倒れていたと思う」。 バンドを取り巻く状況の変化など、多くの要因が重なり、2015年頃にはLEEを除いたメンバーが脱退。「一人やったらバンドもできへんし、いったん区切ろうと思っていた」という時期に、奇跡のように出会ったのが梶原徹也（ドラムス、元THE BLUE HEARTS）、鈴木栄治（ベース、Dachambo）の二人だった。 「やめようと決意した瞬間、二人が目の前に現れたんです。救世主やな、と」。 バンド仲間であったアコーディオン奏者のryotaroも加わり、新たなメンバーでレコーディングを始めるものの、コロナ禍で彼は脱退し、一度中断してしまう。いくつかの不慮の事態を乗り越えつつようやく形になったのが、今回リリースされる新作『カモノハシ』だ。アルバムとしては2012年の『ちんぷんかんぷん』以来、実に14年ぶり。プロデュースとミックスは「“humanERROR”の頃から可愛がってもうてるお父ちゃん的存在であり、いろんなことを教えてくれはる師匠」という久保田麻琴が手掛けている。その久保田が「（喜納昌吉&チャンプルーズの）“ハイサイおじさん”以来の大発見」と太鼓判を押すのが、アルバムの1曲目に収録された“鴨ノ橋”だ。 「京都の通り名を数えていく“丸竹夷”という手毬唄があって、いろんな人がカヴァーしてるんです。そういった歌の伝統を継承しようと思い、僕らは鴨川に架かる橋を数える新しい手毬唄を作ろうと」。

items.body: Label: Sunnyside Records, 2026 Personnel - Lucian Ban: piano; Abraham Burton: tenor saxophone; John Hébert: bass; Eric McPherson: drums; Gavril Tarmure: vocals (#9). Romanian-born pianist and composer Lucian Ban returns with Rush , a refreshingly vital album from his acclaimed group Elevation, featuring saxophonist Abraham Burton, bassist John Hébert, and drummer Eric McPherson. The inspirations come from many sides. The opener, " Dark Blue ”, is a dedication to pianist Abdullah Ibrahim — velvety, comforting contemporary jazz that revels in modal sophistication within an aesthetic that seems to intersect Mingus's ballads and Motian's soft lyric abstraction. Burton speaks wonders here, and I'm especially fond of the way Ban solos, using splendorous harmonic manifestations to accompany himself. " Serenade For Andrew " is a tribute to another great pianist, the inimitable Andrew Hill. Delivered in 3/4, this is solid post-bop with depth, a strong emotional center, and reverence for the man to whom this gripping composition is dedicated. " Christine's Hope " is an Americana-tinged ballad, but the mood lifts with “ Rush ", whose traditionally lilting locomotion, cubist accentuations, imposing pedal points, and rhythmic complexity conjure an amalgamation of Thelonious Monk, Herbie Nichols, Charlie Parker, and Sam Rivers. " Congestion Tax ", improvised spontaneously by the quartet, gradually lends the music its combustive edge, while the delicate " Chakra ", written for Billy Strayhorn, seems to find some solace in Yusef Lateef's Eastern moods. The music is permeated with interplay, sometimes leading to mesmerizing results, as in “Elevation", an achingly beautiful and leisurely illuminated ballad composed for Larry Willis, where the quartet showcases razor-sharp musicianship, sophistication, and passion for sound. Hébert's intimate lyricism is featured here, and the group's spotless dynamics leave us in awe. The journey wraps up with " Golden Oriole ”, a traditional folk song featuring Romanian singer Gavril Tarmure, whose genuine feeling is immediately apparent. He had collaborated with Ban on three folk-jazz crossover pieces included on Songs From Afar (Sunnyside, 2016). These tautly arranged compositions are given fascinating colors, shades, and directions under the captivating performance of Ban's Elevation. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Dark Blue ► 04 - Rush ► 05 - Elevation ► 07 - Chakra

items.body:
BLACKPINK’s JISOO is stepping into character for her latest collaboration with London-based fashion house self-portrait.

Titled Portraits of a Screen Star, the fashion campaign casts JISOO in a series of imagined audition tapes, with the singer and actress taking on four distinct cinematic characters. Shot in Seoul by photographer Oliver Hadlee Pearch, each instalment is set to reveal a different side of her artistry and performance.

The series has premiered with The Enigma, which sees JISOO embodying a curious, whimsical and quietly amused character. For the first instalment, she wears a grey button knit playsuit, a red check frayed knit jacket, and a purple faux leather skirt.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by self-portrait (@mrselfportrait)

Speaking about the project, JISOO shared that the campaign gave her the opportunity to explore something new through each role.

“I was so excited to star in this new series of short films with Han and self-portrait. It allowed me to try something completely new and each character I played required something different from me,” she said.

JISOO added that each character’s wardrobe played an important part in shaping her performances.

“The evolution of the character's wardrobe was how I found the nuance in each performance,” she shared. “I have worn self-portrait for many years and the pieces make me feel like I can do anything — this time, they let me dream that I could be anyone.”

Three more characters, each with their own personality and visual identity, are set to be unveiled throughout September.

items.body:
Idris Elba is bringing his dance-music alter ego to Bangkok.

Performing as IDRIS, the actor, DJ, and producer will take over Cloud 11 Theatre on 26 September for a one-night-only show presented by Collective Minds. The night will also mark the arrival of his record label and music platform, Sound International, in the Thai capital.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Sound International (@sound.intl)

Before becoming internationally known for his acting career, Elba had already found his footing behind the decks. Introduced to DJing by his uncle, who ran a London sound system, he later balanced acting with DJ sets at club night Twice as Nice.

His career as IDRIS has since taken him to Ibiza institutions including Pacha, Pikes, and Hï, as well as festival stages at Glastonbury and Coachella. Behind the decks, he brings together the Afro, calypso, and reggae sounds he grew up with alongside tech-house and progressive rhythms.

Sound International continues that musical lineage. Elba created the label in tribute to his uncle's original sound system, building a home for the global house sound that has shaped his DJ career.

Joining IDRIS at Cloud 11 Theatre are Wildealer and Elaheh, rounding out the lineup for the Bangkok show. Click here to purchase tickets.

items.body:
Hopeful Melodies Pair With Grief & Anxiety-Inspired Lyrics On Lotus Flower's 'A Night of the Jumps'

8 September 2026

When he chose the moniker 'Lotus Flower' for himself, it was clear Shriraj Sagara wasn't trying to hide that he is influenced by Radiohead, his voice often choosing the relaxed, high-pitched falsetto singing that has defined frontman Thom Yorke's work. The Ahmedabad-rooted, Berlin-based musician continues to gradually build upon that influence in his latest EP 'A Night of the Jumps'.

The melodies of the falsetto singing lend more to the atmosphere of synth arpeggios, horn lines and steady percussion rather than inviting the limelight. Meanwhile, Shriraj's compositions carry a more uplifting quality even as they deal with an unsettled mixture of anxiety, grief and vulnerability. Notably, the pounding rhythm section of opener 'Ceremony', unlike the formerly mentioned namesake influence, keeps things more communal and inviting than introspective, even as the song attempts to capture the coldness and disorientation of a difficult winter.

The subtly gritty and detuned synth foundations of 'A Small Town Cries' harken more to the nostalgia found in works by acts like Boards of Canada, though the lyrics draw from fragments of news from Israel's war on Gaza. The track Shriraj join hands again with his brother Shantanu Sagara for another DIY music video, though with less production value than their previous stellar work 'Wilting'.

Check out 'A Night of the Jumps' below and follow Shriraj Sagara on Instagram for more information.

items.body:
Page One

a column by
Bill Shoemaker

Jin Hi Kim: Living Tones


Jim Hi Kim © 2026 Livia Sa




Curating a retrospective of 40 years of recorded music is a daunting task, particularly when it is your own. Accurately representing the arc of the work and the life that created it requires frankness and acceptance. It is a process punctuated with winces and sighs and the occasional grin. Composer and improviser Jin Hi Kim experienced it all when compiling The Jin Hi Kim Collection, recently issued by Neuma. If the use of “odyssey” requires a great voyage, discovering new lands, and encountering titans, then Kim’s journey easily qualifies. Not only did she leave Korea at 23 for the US in 1980, Kim traversed an arguably greater gulf by leaving her elite training in traditional Korean music to study electronic music and composition with Lou Harrison, Terry Riley, and others. In the intervening decades, she worked with leading exponents of contemporary composition and improvisation like Kronos Quartet and Derek Bailey, and transformed the komungo, the traditional five-foot-long lute dating from the 4th Century CE, exponentially extending its sonic range through computer interfaces and signal processing.

Rediscovery accompanied the selection process for the 9-CD Collection. She was especially surprised when reviewing early works transliterating Korean music through Western instruments, or employing graphic notation. “It was created by a young mind,” Kim recently recalled with a laugh. “Sometimes it was hard to hear that’s what I did. But it was also good evidence for an archival collection. It was a wonderful feeling to look at everything I did – well, almost everything – but one thing that I was really proud about it is that there is not just one kind of music. Each piece has its Korean roots but, like I’ve said, I came to America to make new music, so I look at my 40 years of work and, yeah, I achieved that. So, it was a very satisfying process.

“When I listen to some of the improvisations, I realized how young and unafraid I was. Komungo has a limited sound compared to other instruments. When you work with virtuoso improvisers, they have vocabularies that are so rich. They are creating so many different colors and textures, but komungo has limits. It doesn’t allow you to express so much of the story. It has a meditative energy, of nothingness, of slowness. I was so brave to use this instrument with such incredible masters and to communicate with them and create music with them. I did it somehow with my inner energy. I was able to present this inner energy.”

The Collection almost equally divides Kim’s work in composition and improvisation, with five discs devoted to works for orchestra and chamber music ensembles, and four documenting improvisations with, among others, an impressive diversity of percussionists, including Gerry Hemingway, Susie Ibarra, and Tony Oxley, and string players like Bill Frisell, Min Xiao-Fen, and Hans Reichel. If anything can be read into it, the slight tilt reflects her ardent pursuit to articulate the concept of Living Tones Compositions, and how central it is to her work.

“The most important thing about the Living Tones Compositions is to convey the Korean element and philosophy through Western contemporary music,” she explained. “When I came to the United States after training in traditional Korean music, European classical music was more respected in Korea than the traditional music. They didn’t know much about American avant-garde music then, in the 1970s. I was a young musician who trained with the very best teachers and saw that I was not respected because I was not doing Western music.

“That created within me a great desire to fix that problem. You can’t fix anything, but I was young, I had a passion and a mission. I was living in the United States; I was composing for Western musicians; so how could I make this Korean idea, this Korean state of mind in making music, how could I put this together with Western music with equal respect? That was my thing. All my Living Tones Compositions come from the idea of putting together the Korean context and philosophy and Western instruments and musical context, to see how Western musicians took to the Korean attitude – not necessarily techniques, scales, anything like that – but this attitude, this state of mind. That’s what I’m doing with Living Tones music.

“Korean traditional music was once influenced by Chinese music,” Kim prefaced to explain the context and philosophy of Korean music, which she also detailed extensively in her book, Duality of Ancient Korean Roots and Western New Music. “Korean music can be divided into folk music and court music. Court music was quite different from music of ordinary people. The court was deeply influenced by ancient Chinese philosophy – yin and yang; the five elements, and ancient ancestors worship. The music wasn’t entertainment; it was ritual – that was part of both court and folk music. For ordinary people, they associated music with the shaman. For court music, there were virtuoso musicians who created an austere music, based on a philosophy of cosmic sound and abstract thinking; but for ordinary people, the shaman always took care of pain, community pain. Music was performed for celebrations of harvests and other things, but more for problems like drought, someone who is sick, some kind of problem. The shaman is always dealing with the problem of pain in their lives. They always had to sing something very sad. Her song has nothing to do with joyous things – always grief and pain. Ordinary people related to that.

“Both court and folk music had an emphasis on energy – they never thought of music as just sound. It had healing energy. In the folk community, they tried to imitate the shaman, the way she sang, shaking the notes, trying to reach out to another spirit, trying to connect heaven and earth. If you listen to a shaman’s song, there’s a very strong vibrato. The instrumentalists who don’t sing listen to this type of music; it’s very touching, very soulful, and it reflects the problems in their lives. Korean instrumentalists are all shaking, shaking their hands, shaking their instruments, shaking their notes. I play komungo, where the strings can move a lot, up and down, so you can really shake the notes and express the music in the same way as the shaman. I translate that process, that context, that spirit, into Living Tones. Each tone has its own light, and because it has its own light, its time is elastic. It is not like abstract Western time, where you count the time of each note perfectly, and you don’t have the space for microtones. There’s no time to do that in Western music. Time becomes much more open and that’s why in Korean music they don’t talk about abstract time but time in a cycle. Within that cycle, you have a lot of freedom of how to use that space with deep vibratos or any other articulation to create that intense feeling.”

The qualities Kim ascribes to Korean music are manifest in the komungo. It has a palpably plangent sound, with a bass register lower and more resonant than the guembri’s and the sting of ancient harps in its highest notes.  It has a timbral luster comparable to the dark, iridescent glazes of pit-fired ceramics or the blocks of deep color that hover over the black basecoats of a Mark Rothko painting. Its dredge-like twang and the skeletal figures central to the music stop the racing, associative Western mind dead in its tracks. Even before Kim augmented the instrument with signal processing, Western improvisers had a strong attraction to the komungo. Conversely, improvisation has, over the decades, impacted Kim’s outlook.

However, Kim has a nuanced view on how improvisation has influenced her. “Influence is the result over a long period,” she elaborated, “because I played with a person one time or two times. That long period is a really deep space. It’s not that a particular musician gave me something. It is that the experience of playing with someone becomes part of my life experience. Now I look at something differently than when I was young. I understand how the universe works because of scientists and I understand how improvisation works because of improvisers. When you travel all around the world – I’ve performed in over 60 countries and have lived in some of these countries for a long time, six months or even a year – then you have an incredibly different life perspective. All of those things interest me. So, I have been influenced by many things over the decades, so that when I play with someone, it is not just that moment I am responding to; it’s everything about the other musicians: their instruments; their traditions; their culture. That gives me a very clear idea what to do.

“When I was young, I was so desperate to communicate successfully with each improviser I played with. I was trying to understand their personality; I was trying to understand their vocabulary. There have been very few times that I played on the spot without any information about the people I was playing with. I had heard them before I had the opportunity to play with them, playing with other musicians or solo. In my own way, I understood who they are. If I don’t understand them and their musical elements, I have no way to contribute anything on komungo. I have to understand their personality, their energy, how they process the music. Not all people process the same way; some people are poetic; some people are very emotional; some people are very funny. Everybody has those things happening. Understanding that was very important to me. It helped me to communicate, to hear what they were giving me, so I could give back. I listened a lot to what they were doing at a particular moment.”

Given that improvisers spanning James Newton and Elliott Sharp, and Rüdiger Carl and Oliver Lake, are heard throughout the box set, it is noteworthy that Kim singles one out to illustrate her approach to improvisation. “When I work with William Parker, he has a very deep energy in his soul,” she said of the bassist. “When I played with him, he influenced me with his deep energy.  It’s really big. That influenced me to be really big. That bigness, that abundance, that tireless energy; that lets us play a really long time. He has the qualities to do something that a Korean shaman could do, playing the same idea over and over and over for a long time – trance like – but the energy becomes more powerful. William Parker has that type of energy. The bass is like the komungo; it has a deep energy and incredible power. I’m really influenced by that.”

Retrospectives like the Collection are generally considered to be merely summations, but in Kim’s case, it is more a marker of distance travelled and journeys ahead. “It reflects my continuous evolution as an artist. Throughout my musical journey, I have always searched for new ways to express myself creatively while remaining deeply rooted in my Korean musical identity.

“In essence, every work in this collection is the result of my enduring desire to elevate often-neglected Korean aesthetics, shaped alongside the freedom I found in America – a place that allowed me to pursue my artistic passions and ideas without limitation.

“Today, my perspective extends beyond national boundaries to the increasingly interconnected global community. I have aspired to use music as a spiritual and transformative force to confront social challenges. I believe this has become the new direction of my artistic journey.”

Kim’s new direction has steered her towards to uplifting marginalized subalterns and breaking through the fourth wall of the concert hall separating musicians from listeners. “Right now, because the world has changed so much, and America is now so blue, and so many people are mentally ill – I know because I recently gave a music meditation workshop at the Yale mental health center – I want to do something about community pain. I always go back to what the shaman does. I think I have sort of achieved my goal of blending Korean and Western ways of thinking with Living Tones, so right now I want to make music that the community participates in. Not necessarily well-trained musicians, but anybody who is interested. I already started on this in 2023 with a piece called ‘Ritual for Earth.’ I would like to do these things for now. I’m not anxious about my career or my next commission. I’m thinking about community pain, environmental issues like wildfires and floods, the world we are living in. So, if I have the opportunity, working with communities is what I want to do.”
